speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think that you and the members of this House can only come to the conclusion that, although the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) was specifically critical in many of his remarks, yet, in the general sense he commended the actions of the committee. As his strongest complaint was about the lack of rules given to the committee in the first place, and against the want of rules which guided the committee in the division of the different towns and cities. I will, for a moment, refer to that part of his speech. In the first place, I fail to see how it can be possible that any more than a general rule can be laid down for the division of a constituency. But the hon. gentleman complains that the leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden, Halifax) did lay before the committee certain rules under which we were asked to divide the constituencies in Ontario, and that the committee refused to adopt those rules. I purpose taking these rules one by one, and I think that I can give to the House and the country good and sufficient reason for the non-adoption of those rules by a majority of the committee. On June 26th, at a meeting of the committee, the leader of the opposition, as reported in the report of the committee's proceedings, page 146, said :
Mr. Chairman, the resolutions which are being proposed with regard to Ontario are practically the same as those which have already been suggested at the informal meetings of the committee. The only difference, I think, is the calculations with respect to the unit having been made as they were made when the proposition was presented in the first instance. At that time, the unit was not worked out ; ill this it is worked out.

He tlaen handed in the following resolution respecting the distribution of Ontario :
In accordance with the principles laid down by the Prime Minister in the House on the introduction of the Bill, the municipal county boundaries shall be observed.
I have only to say, in regard to that rule, that while the committee were quite prepared to accept that rule in a general sense and prepared to say the county boundaries should be adhered to, they were not prepared to accept that rule in the full sense. The Minister of Public Works (Hon. Mr. Sutherland) put the matter fairly in saying, as he did :
I do not know that we should bind ourselves, if we found we were doing an unfair thing to a certain section of the people. But I understand that the intention of the Prime Minister was, that municipal county boundaries should be adhered to, and not departed from for the purpose of political advantage.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Will the hon. gentleman (Mr. Hyman) permit me to ask him-how many constituencies are there in the Bill we are now considering in which county boundaries have not been adhered to ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
I shall come to that point in a moment. Had we adopted the rule proposed by the leader of the opposition, we should have found ourselves unable to depart, in any instance from the county boundaries. But at almost the next meeting, the committee unanimously decided to depart from county boundaries in one or two instances. So far as the county of Renfrew was concerned, it was felt by the committee that the three townships of Clara, Head and Maria should be removed from Renfrew and placed with Nipissing. This was not done for political purposes, and it was unanimously agreed to. Then, it was decided that the townships of Osgoode and Gloucester should be taken from the county of Carleton and placed in Russell, and not only the members of the government side, but the members of the opposition concurred. The only other instance which I can recall in which county boundaries were departed from was the township of South Monaghan, which is municipally connected with the county of Northumberland, and which was, for the purposes of representation in this House, placed in Peterborough. That also was unanimously accepted by the committee as a fair proposition. So, the majority saw nothing to be gained by refusing to adopt the rule proposed by the leader of the opposition ; they simply did not want to stultify themselves when they came to these three particular instances which nobody could charge were done for party purposes, and they did not wish to bind themselves hard and fast.
Rule 2,
Where separate representation is given to cities, municipal boundaries in such cities shall be observed.
Now, see the hair-splitting here. Why observe boundaries in cities when they have a representation themselves ? Why not observe the boundaries of all cities ? Why simply say : Observe the boundary of a city which has a special representation, but if the city happens to come under the unit of population, we won't observe the boundaries ? For that reason, and I think the House and the country will bear me out.In the statement, the committee were right not to coniine themselves to that hard and fast rule. Nor could the members of the opposition upon the committee be so confined, they must have looked ahead for when they came to the county of Elgin they themselves proposed to divide the city of St. Thomas, and their proposition is before the House in the shape of one of the amendments introduced by the leader of the opposition. Well, why should St. Thomas be divided and why should the city of Toronto not be divided ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I would like to point out to the hon. gentleman that there seems to be-a mistake. The hon. gentlemen themselves who were on the committee had four propositions, none of which were made by any of the Conservatives.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I am speaking subject to correction, but I understand that the official proposition which is made from the opposition involves the division of the city of St. Thomas.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: That is certainly what we understood the hon. gentleman to say.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: We understand him now to say that there was a proposition from the opposition.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: No, I say there must have been something in the minds of hon. gentleman when they laid this rule down, which I think is not general in its application.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: We understood him to say a minute ago that a proposition emanated from this side of the House, or from the committee representing this side of the House, that the city of St. Thomas should be divided.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I think that does emanate from the opposite side of the House ; I may be wrong.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I wish to point out to the hon. gentleman that there were four propositions before the committee, all of which emanated from the Liberal party. Seeing that the Liberal party proposed to divide St. Thomas, then the opposition suggested a way by which they could do it better than the one the Liberals proposed.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I am glad that the mem-I bers of the opposition sometimes accept good

speechtext: Emanating from the Liberal party.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
I do not wish to discuss that matter, these amendments were accepted, anyway. Now, Mr. Speaker, I have given reasons why the committee would not adopt rule 2. Now let us take rule 3 :
The municipal county boundaries shall be those set forth in chapter 3, Revised Statutes of Canada, 1897, and that the word * county ' herein shall include any provisional county or territorial district established by the said Act.
Those are the very words which appear in the Bill, which is the official report of'the committee, and which is now before the House.
Rule (b.) The separate representation to be allotted to cities of Ontario shall be first fixed and determined before proceeding with the representation of the rural constituencies.
Now, Mr. Speaker, that rule must be taken in connection with rule (d.) :
The population of any city receiving separate representation shall be excluded in computing the population of the county within which it is situate.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I do not know whether the hon. gentlemen who brought these rules into the House understood their effect, for they might just as well have said that in the county of Middlesex you must exclude the city of London from the population of the county before you apply representation to that county, because that rule applies solely to the county of Middlesex, it is not general in its application. There seems to have been something hidden under it, and for that reason I think the Minister of Public works very properly said, although the opposition seemed to think he was wrong :
Mr. Chairman, I can hardly say, as a member of this committee, -whether I would agree to dissent to this proposition. It is a long document, involving one can hardlv tell what unless it vras worked out.
I think he was perfectly right, because this is not general ill its application at all, it ap-Mr. HYMAN.
plies only to one county when worked out, to the county of Middlesex and to the city of London ; and for that reason I think the committee were perfectly justified in refusing to be bound by a hard and fast rule of that kind.
Rule (c.) The unit of representation for such rural constituencies shall be determined by deducting from the total population of Ontario the combined population of the said cities, and by dividing the remainder by the total number of seats to be allotted to rural constituencies.
Well, what is involved in this rule ? It involves the division of all the cities of Ontario in an arbitrary manner. Now, it hast been well said that there is just one city ir Ontario, the city of Toronto, which the com mittee have treated arbitrarily, and it was felt by the committee that in fixing the unit of population, the city of Toronto only, as being the only city treated arbitrarily, should be deducted from the total population and then the division should be made by the number of members allotted to the province deducting the five members for Toronto. For that reason the committee refused to adopt that rule. I may say that in working out this rule, the unit was adopted unanimously by the committee, and the unit of representation in Ontario was fixed at 24,381. fixed unanimously by the committee, and fixed by deducting from the total population of Ontario the population of Toronto, and dividing the remainder by the number of members that remained for Ontario, namely, 81.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Does the hon. gentleman mean to say that the committee were unanimous in applying the arbitrary rule to the city of Toronto ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
No, I made no such statement. The next rule reads as follows :
The redistribution of the representation of Ontario shall then be determined as follows -
Counties having a population below the unit
(a.) Each county having a population of not less than two-thirds of the unit shall be entitled to one member.
I may say that the rule was followed out in every instance by the committee.
Rule (b.) Any county not entitled to one member shall be added to that adjoining county to which it is related as a judicial district, or with which it is connected for judicial or municipal purposes, and the representation of such combined counties shall be dealt with upon the principles already and hereinafter stated.
Now, Mr. Speaker, a reference to the population of the different counties in Ontario would have been a very simple thing, and! it would have been found that there was only one county in Ontario which lias less than two-thirds of the unit which would entitle it to representation, and that county is the provisional district of Haliburtou. So that the rule might just as well have read that the provisional district of Haliburtou

should be joined to the county of Victoria, because it happened to be judicially connected with that county. Now, that is not a general rule. It is a rule which is vague in its meaning, and I think the Liberal members of the committee were perfectly right in not adopting these rules until they saw how they would work out. In that case, it meant joining Haliburton to Victoria, and by so doing, giving Victoria a larger representation in this House than it is entitled to if left by itself. For that reason we did not see our way to adopt that rule.
Rule (a.)-Each county or combined county having a population of not less than fifty per cent and not more than one hundred and fifty per cent above the unit shall be entitled to two members, and each county or combined county having a population of not less than 150 per cent and not more than 250 per cent above the unit shall be entitled to three members.
Afterwards that rule was practically carried out.
(b.) If after applying these principles it is found that any seats remain to be allotted, such seats shall be allotted to the counties or combined counties approaching most closely to the conditions which, under the above rule, would entitle them to additional representation.
That rule was practically adopted. The next rule is as follows :
In the division of cities or counties into ridings the geographical limits of such ridings shall be as symmetrical and compact as may be possible, always having regard to equalities of population.
I think that when the Bill is before the Committee of the Whole House it will be found that that rule has practically been carried out. Now, there were eleven rules before the committee. The hon. member for Jacques Carties complains very bitterly that we have failed to comply with these rules In making a summary of these rules I find that five rules which were of general application were acted upon by the committee, that there were three rules which treated large cities other than Toronto in an arbitrary way as far as representation is concerned aud which were not in accordance with the wishes of the committee. Therefore these three rules were not accepted. Two of the rules were not general in their application, one affecting solely the county of Middlesex and the other affecting solely the county of \ ictoria and the majority refused to adopt them. The remaining rule was the rule which the committee afterwards unanimously departed from in the cases in which it departed from county boundaries to which I have referred. I am perfectly prepared to leave the whole question as to whether these rules should have been accepted by the committee or whether they should not have been accepted with the reasons I have given to the judgment of the House and of the country and I feel quite sure that the House and the country
will conclude that we have done nothing unfair in regard to these rules and that we have not made any departure from any of the principles laid down by the right lion, leader of the government in moving the second reading of this Bill. Now, the hon. member for Jacques Cartier, after making some general statements, made two or three particular references to the division of counties in Ontario. As the hon. gentlemen who have already spoken have only referred to Waterloo and Middlesex, with the exception that the hon. member for Jacques Cartier made some reference to the county of Hastings, I suppose it is only fair to presume that the opposition think that in regard to these two counties, or possibly in regard to these three counties, they have the greatest cause for complaint. I can only give to the House the reason why, in the first place, the division that was made of the county of Waterloo was agreed to by the majority of the committee and I feel quite sure that the majority of the House will admit when I have given the reasons to the House that the committee under all the circumstances did only that which was right and fair and just by the county of Waterloo. In^the first place the whole matter depends upon the question whether this House is prepared to lay down the principle that in the redistribution of the constituencies of Ontario, townships shall be cut in two. The hon. member for Jacques Cartier lamented the fact that the House had not laid down more principles when the Bill went to the committee, but what would have been, said by the hon. gentleman without having any knowledge of the division likely to be made in the county of Waterloo if the right hon. leader of the government had laid it down as a principle upon which the committee might act that it might cut townships in two ? I feel quite sure that the hon. gentleman on reflecting for a moment will see quite plainly that to lay down such a principle would be unfair. When this matter of the division of the county of Waterloo came before the committee, in so far as I am concerned and in so far as the majority of the committee is concerned, we felt that we should not carve aud cut a township in two where it was possible to make a fair representation, without so doing. If you lay down the principle that a township shall not be cut in two,
I do not think there is one hon. gentleman in this House who can raise one single exception to the division of the county of Waterloo as embodied in the report of the committee which has been brought before this House. I do not think there is any other possible way to divide the county of Waterloo providing you lay down the principle that a county shall not be cut in two. In considering the question of the division of the county of Waterloo I happened to be reading over one of the old debates of 1892 and I read from the remarks made by a

very prominent member of this House. 1 am sorry the hon. gentleman is not in his seat at the present moment. I refer to the hon. member for North Victoria (Mr. Hughes). The hon. gentleman was good enough this morning to call across the House and ask whether the hon. member for London had seen the division of the county of Waterloo. I would ask the hon. member for North Victoria if he were here if lie has seen the division of Waterloo because he is reported in ' Hansard ' of June 8, 1892, as' having made certain references to the division of that county. He spoke as follows :
Hon. gentlemen also see the fantastic shape of South Waterloo

When I refer to South Waterloo, I am referring to the South Waterloo which the hon. member for Jacques Cartier so theatrically placed on the Table this morning.
Hon. gentlemen can also see .the fantastic shape of South Waterloo. That the House may properly appreciate how South Waterloo is doctored up and to what extremes these purists of the Liberal party will go to gerrymander a county, I shall read you a description of the county of Waterloo from the Revised Statutes of Ontario.
Unfortunately the hon. gentleman was not aware of the fact that the division of Waterloo for provincial purposes and the division for representation in tiiis parliament was exactly the same. I think we may say under these circumstances that we have a fair and honest opinion and we will give the hon. gentleman credit for having given a fair and honest opinion. He proceeds :
I shall read you a description of the county of Waterloo from the Revised Statutes of Ontario, and you will notice that, not content with dividing the municipalities, they even divide lots, and in some places where there is a good old Tory with four or live sons, they draw a line around his lot and hedge him off into another riding in order that he may not do any injury by his vote to the Reform party. This is the description of the county from the Act itself.
And then follows the description of the county.

speechtext:
Lt.-Col. Hughes was the member, I understand. Under these circumstances, we can* quite conceive that when the committee approached the question of the division of Waterloo the view of the majority very largely conformed to the criticism which this hon. gentleman had placed on record. To go further into particulars, I wish to call attention to one or two facts. The county of Waterloo, as divided by the committee, is called North and South Waterloo. North Waterloo consists of the townships of Waterloo, the towns of Berlin, Hespeler and Waterloo, and the village of Preston. South AVater-loo consists of the townships of North Dumfries, AVellesley, .Wilmot and AVoolwicli, the town of Galt and the villages of Ayr, Elmira and New Hamburg. In the redistri-bU'tion of 1881, owing to the differences of population, it was not possible to make the division of the county which the committee has made now, and for this reason : In 1881, South Waterloo, as we propose to divide it, had a population of 26,909 and North Waterloo had a population of only 15,831. When the division was made in 1882, therefore, the conditions as to population were entirely different. There would have been a difference in the population of those two ridings, had the same division been made as now, of over 11,000, and such a division would have been unfair then in every sense of the word. In 1892 it was still not possible to make the present suggested division, for the reason that in 1891 the population of the south riding had only grown from 26,909 to 29,429, and the north riding had only grown to 21,035. If this division had been made then it would have involved a difference of 8,000 between the populations of the two ridings. But, Sir, in 1901 the population of the proposed south riding has fallen from 29 429 to 27,438, and the population of the so-called north riding has risen from 21,035 to 25.156. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, for the first time in the history of any redistribution it becomes possible to give the township of AAraterloo a member to itself, as I submit it is entitled to. The growth of population has in the last decade been confined almost entirely to the township of Waterloo ; in fact, the other part of Waterloo has decreased in population ; and, therefore, I think that the committee would hav.e done less than its duty if it did not give the township of Waterloo a member. If the committee had not done so, the people could well reproach this parliament for failing to give them a member, as they are entitled to one by population. Then, Sir, there is no riding in Canada, outside of a city riding, where the community of interest is as great as it is in the township of Waterloo. Those of us who are acquainted with

that township know perfectly wiell that there are the following large manufacturing towns in it: Hespeler, with a population of 2,457 ; Preston, with a population of 2,308 ; Waterloo, with a population of 3,537 ; Berlin, with a population of 9,747, or a total urban population in that township of 18,049. Iteanember that there is an urban population sufficiently large, if they were all in the one city, to entitle it to representation under the principle laid down by the leader of the opposition before the committee. In view of the community of interest ; in view of the large urban population in that township ; in view of the opinion of the hon. member for North Victoria (Mr. Hughes), and with our knowledge of the growth, of population in one riding as compared with the other ; I cannot see how any serious attack can be made upon the committee's work in regard to that particular instance, unless we are prepared to accept the cutting in tw'o of townships as being justified in a general sense.
The other particular reference made by the hon. member (Mr. Monk) was with regard to the county of Middlesex. The county of Middlesex has a population of 92,702, and the general complaint made by the hon. member (Mr. Monk) was that that county, under this Bill, is given three representatives, whereas three or four other counties with a larger population are only given two representatives each. But how did the hon. gentleman arrive at the population of the county of Middlesex ? He took the total population of the county and deducted therefrom the population of the city of London, thus treating the city of London in an arbitrary wTajr, so far as its representation is concerned. Middlesex has a population of 92,702 and the city of London lias a population of 37,976. If you make two units of that, London with 37,970 and Middlesex with 54,726, the city of Loudon is entitled to two representatives and the county of Middlesex is entitled to two representatives. But the very rule which these hon. gentlemen opposite desired us to adopt in committee would have forced us to have given only one member to the city of London and two members only to the county of Middlesex. But why, in placing the members, should you deduct the population of the city from the total population of the county before placing these members ? If Middlesex has 92,702, surely it ought to be taken as a unit, and therefore it should get the number of members it is entitled to, taking into consideration the unit for the whole province. I am sure there should be no departure from that rule, and I feel quite satisfied that the House and the country will bear me out in laying down that proposition. I cannot discover why the city of London should be the only city in Canada which the members of the opposition upon the committee desire to treat in an arbitrary fashion. The
official amendment which hon. gentlemen opposite have given notice of, notwithstanding the fact that the city of London has a population of 37,976, still persists in giving to that constituency but one representative. It is only right and fair that the county of Middlesex, having a population of 92,702, is entitled to a representation of four members in this House, because taking the unit and applying the principle as laid down in the. committee, the unit entitles it to that representation. I take the responsibility on my shoulders very largely, as I represent a portion of the county of Middlesex, and the reason why we did not give London two members and the county of Middlesex two members is simply this:	If you gave London, with its
population of 37,907, two members, the unit for the city of London would be a little under 19,000, and if you gave the county of Middlesex only two members the unit for the coipity of Middlesex would be something like 27.000. That would seem hardly fair, because the county of Middlesex at present is represented by four members, and as the city of London is represented only by one member, it did seem hardly fair that under all the circumstances we should take two members from the representation of Middlesex and give the city of London one extra member. These are the reasons why the committee dealt with the county of Middlesex in that particular way.	.

In British Columbia, where there are seven electoral divisions, the committee agree upon the division of Kootenay, and practically upon Yale-Cariboo. In New Westminster, the only difference is on the question of including a part of the district of Yale. I may say that this particular part of the district of Yale extends over the mountain, and is contiguous in every way to New Westminster. The reason the committee had for adopting the division they did was that two members from British Columbia, the hon. senior member for Victoria (Mr. Earle) and the hon. member for New Westminister (Mr. Morrison), both appeared before the committee, and they agreed in saying that this is a proper division to make. In Vancouver the only question was the inclusion or exclusion of the suburbs of the city of Vancouver. And here again I may say, the committee were favoured with the attendance of the hon. senior member for Victoria. who agreed that it was right and pro-

speechtext: My statement before that committee was simply this, that if the principles laid down by the First Minister, that we were to be governed by municipal boundaries and by an effort to equalize the population, were to be governing principles, then my suggestion to the committee was on the lines of both those principles. It is not my intention at the present moment to discuss more than the principle of the Bill. We will have lots of opportunities of discussing the question in detail in the committee and when we have fully threshed it out in committee and evolved some principle as the result of our efforts we will then have an opportunity of speaking on the question on a future time. But, I want to say a few words on the principle of the Bill as it is being discussed at the present moment. The committee was named at the instance of the right hon. gentleman who leads the government (Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Eaurier). I was in the House at the time and I remember the statement that he made. He instanced the interview between Lord Salisbury and Mr. Gladstone which took place in i SSI and he stated that at that time there was a conference between these two parties for the purpose of settling the representation in Great Britain. The right hon. gentleman stated in introducing this Bill that it was his policy to call a conference and. to submit the Bill to it. So much was I impressed with the statement of the right hon. gentleman, because I knew what a conference meant, that I was favourably impressed by it. In my mind a conference meant that the 341*
parties to It would come to a unanimous decision. It meant a compromise of the different parties in the House in reference to the matter submitted to it. The right hon. gentleman afterwards named a committee witli the agreement, I believe, of the hon. gentleman who leads the opposition (Mr. Borden, Halifax) as to the personnel of the committee and to that committee was submitted the Bill, or was submitted the duty of preparing a Bill to be brought down to this House. Now, when I became a member of that committee my friends on this side of the House knew well, because the proposal was considered by them privately, what my views were on the matter. I urged upon them the acceptance of the committee for the purpose of considering this measure. I stated that we had the authority of the right hon. gentleman for the belief that this was in fact to be a conference the same as that which had guided the two parties in England in framing the representation in the British House of Commons. A great many of my friends differed with me. I find to my sorrow that they were right. They told me that it would be no conference but that it would be a committee of the House and that the majority would rule. I took my right hon. friend at his word believing that this committee was to be a committee having the character of a conference for the purpose of coming to a fair conclusion as a matter of compromise between the several parties in the country as to what would be a proper representation of the country in parliament. I know that when the matter was submitted to the committee we had very few instructions. The only instruction that was given us to guide us was the statement of the right hon. gentleman that municipal boundaries should be as nearly as possible adhered to and that everything that was done to make an equitable redistribution according to county boundaries on the principles of equity would be agreed to by the committee; and that the government had no other wish. I hope the right hon. gentleman when he hears the full details of the proceedings of this committee will recall the statement that he made when he introduced the Bill, because, when it is brought to his attention that there was not a single compromise between the two parties on the committee and that not a single proposition that was made by hon. gentlemen representing this side of the House was accepted, he will see how very little attention was paid to the pledge which he gave upon that occasion. No matter what evidence was brought before the committee, no matter what proposition was made by hon. gentlemen representing this side of the House before the committee, no attention was paid to them. The committee brought in a report as if it had been agreed to before hand. When a question in reference to a constituency came up before the committee

no attention was paid to them. The committee brought in a report as if it had been agreed to beforehand. When a question in reference to a constituency came up before the committee the member for the constituency was summoned before the committee, his evidence was taken and what was the result ? As far as the Conservative constituency was concerned in which a change in the representation was required not one of the statements of any member representing such a Conservative constituency, not any of the evidence that was adduced before the committee, had the slightest weight with or influence upon the opinions of the majority of the committee. What was the course in England ? What was tlie principle adopted in the conference between Mr. Gladstone and Lord Salisbury ? The members of the government under Mr. Gladstone met the leader of the opposition, Lord Salisbury, and I think Sir Stafford Northcote accompanied them and the principles that were to be submitted to the committee appointed for the delimitation of the different * constituencies were agreed upon between them. The first consideration was as to what was to be the unit of representation, and the next, as to whether the urban population was entitled to greater representation than the rural population. Then they considered, whether, in dividing the constituencies a part of the urban population should be attached to the towns and cities, or allowed to remain with the boroughs and counties. Instructions as to delimitation were submitted to the committee. The committee of delimitation urns not composed of members of the House of Commons, but was selected by Sir William Hareourt, then a minister of the Crown. The committee got their instructions from the government of the day in line with the agreement made between the Marquis of Salisbury, Sir Stafford Northcote, and others. It was submitted to the committee that municipal or parish boundaries were to be adhered to, that there should be equality of population so far as possible, that the constituencies were to be bunched together so far as might be, and there was no different unit for the urban and rural population.

speechtext:
In the English Act of 1885, the unit of representation for the boroughs and the cities was the same. It is true that under the decision of the commissioners, some of the urban constituencies had a large unit of population to the extent of one-half more, and sometimes double that of the rural constituencies; but that was caused by the configuration of the district, and by the harmony of interests which were involved. But the 'principle was adopted, that a man who resided in an urban constituency should have as Hon. Mr. HAGGART.
much value attached to his vote as the man who resides in a rural constituency. Of course that is a different doctrine from that laid down by a former leader of the Conservative party in Canada. His doctrine was, that on account of the number of members representing rural constituencies who resided in cities, and on account of the greater number of senators who resided in cities, the urban population had more influence in parliament than had the rural population, and the same unit of representation should not be applied to them. However, a different principle was adopted in England, viz : That the unit of population should be nearly the same in urban as in rural constituencies. Now, in the committee, the report of which we are now considering, the minority proposed what they thought was the fairest possible principle that could be adopted for the purpose of delimiting the constituencies in Ontario. First of all, we made the proposition that county boundaries should be adopted. I was anxious to find out what ' county ' meant under the Interpretation Act, and the Minister of Justice stated that county boundaries were such as were described by the Municipal Act of the province of Ontario. I drew his attention to the fact that there were several united counties, such as Leeds and Grenville, Fron-tenac, Lennox and Addington, and Stormont, Dundas and Glengarry. From the manner iu which the Minister of Justice spoke, I thought that there was no doubt that we had an understanding as to what county boundaries meant, but to my astonishment, when we came to delimit the counties, the question was raised as to whether it would not be possible where there were two or three members representing a united county, that county boundaries within the united counties should be adhered to. The committee, after a good deal of hesitation, and not without the minority compromising its position to a certain extent, agreed to stick to county boundaries even within the boundaries of united counties. The other principles that were involved in that proposition were not agreed to, at the instance of the Minister of Public Works (Hon. Mr. Sutherland). He would not be bound to a hard and fast rule. The principle was to have elasticity where it was necessary, and the hon. member for London (Mr. Hyman) now tells us that that principle has been very seldom departed from. Well, that elasticity gave the majority power, in a province like Ontario, to so delimit the boundaries-and I am afraid they have used that power to the fullest extent-that notwithstanding the predominating popular Conservative majority in Ontario they could see to it that a Reform majority was returned to this House. I think, Sir, that when the people of Canada understand that thoroughly they will place a different interpretation on the conduct of the majority in the committee, from what these gentle-

men think. I hold that the result of any attempt of that kind in any province of the Dominion, will be adverse to the party who attempts it. We have been often taunted with doing something of that kind in 1882, but as my hon. friend from Halton (Mr. Henderson) has proven, we did nothing of the kind. We did not have any greater representation in the House of Commons than we were entitled to by the Conservative majority in the province.

It was not like the gerrymander, the Redistribution Bill, of the local legislature by which, although there is an adverse popular majority against the party in power, that party manages to maintain a majority in the House.
I said before, that I would not discuss this Bill fully now, as I intend to discuss it in detail at another stage. I wish, however, to show the result of the meetings of the conference or committee, and what was forced down our throats by that committee. I shall refer now only to two points which have been dealt with by the hon. member for London (Mr. Hyman), one in reference to my own county of Lanark and the other in reference to his own constituency, the coun-,ty of Middlesex. In order to obtain an undue representation for Middlesex he was obliged to add the population of the city of London to the population of the county of Middlesex. All of the cities of Ontario, London, Hamilton, Ottawa, Toronto, Kingston, were dealt with on a different basis from the suburban population ; their population was separated from the counties. If you separate the population of London from that of the county of Middlesex, you cannot, by any reasoning in the world, show that Middlesex is -entitled to more than two members. In reference to the county of Lanark, the hon. gentleman says that I proposed the addition of North Sherbrooke to South Lanark. Any person who is acquainted with the map of the county of Lanark knows what the township of Sherbrooke is. It has a broken line along the old united county of Frontenac, Lennox and Addington-Lennox and Addington as It is now. The dividing line Is a different line from the township boundary, and the consequence is that the base of South Sherbrooke, which is In South Lanark is hardly ten miles, and yet Sherbrooke runs up to a point that is twenty miles north from the base. Across the middle of that township it is now proposed to separate South Sherbrooke from North Sherbrooke; I simply asked that the whole township of Sherbrooke should be included in South Lanark. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Hyman) forgot to state that at the time I made that proposition I also made a proposition which was suggested to me by the hon. Minister of Public Works (Hon. Mr. Sutherland), that is the addition of Beckwith to North Lanark. If the township of Beckwith was added to North Lanark-and if my hon. friend will look at my remarks before the committee he will see that I made that suggestion-it would be a counterpoise to Sherbrooke. The population of Sherbrooke, as he says, is only a little above 300. He says it has a voting power of 60 or 70, and that these are practically all supporters of the right hon. gentleman and his friends on that side of the House. Admitting that, I was willing to take them into my riding, as there are in South Lanark such an overwhelming number of Conservative voters that it would make no difference.

The addition of Lieckwith to North Lanark would be a gain that would at least balance any political difference made by the adding of North Sherbrooke to South Lanark, and the effect of it would have been to make the populations of the two ridings as nearly as possible equal. I do not care much about the report of the committee as far as it affects my own constituency. South Lanark is the same as for the local, and the change will not affect me, politically, in the least. By the proposed Bill, two townships, Fitzroy and Huntley are taken off the North riding and put in the old county of Carle-ton, to which they formerly belonged and the town of Carleton Place is added to North Lanark. Possibly with this change my hon. friend from North Lanark (Mr. Rosamond) will not be in as good a position, politically, as he was with Carleton Place in my riding and Fitzroy and Huntley attached to North Lanark. However, with the sins which the right hon. gentleman and his followers have committed during the last two or three years, I think that our chances in North Lanark, which is always a fighting constituency, will be better in the future than they have been in the past, even with the changes made. I do not intend now to deal with any details except with reference to these two particular ridings, but when the Bill is in committee I intend to discuss every alteration which has been made, and I believe that notwithstanding the statements of the hon. member for London in supporting the Bill, that when the Bill is in committee and its glaring inconsistencies are pointed out to the right hon. the Premier, he will feel it his duty to himself and to the House, after the statements he made in introducing the Bill, to agree to such alterations as will make the Bill not the result of the work of a committee of which a majority were friends of the right hon. gentleman with a political leaning in his favour, but a Bill framed in the light of the proposition made by the right hon. gentleman in introducing it, according to the principle which is adopted in England at the present day, in

accordance with the principle which must prevail in this country if we intend to have any fair government, the principle that representation by population must prevail without consideration of the political advantage of parties. The only consideration should be community of interest, segregation of population, and as nearly as possible, equality of population. This must be the result and must be the finality of all Redistribution Bills in this country if they are to have the honest, moral support of the community ; they must be as fair to one side as to the other, and in order to accomplish this we must adopt the principle which was adopted in England or else adopt the principle laid down by Sir Charles Tup-per in his amendment to the Bill proposed three or four sessions ago, that a tribunal removed from political influence shall perform the delimitation of all the constituencies according to certain rules. I have no objection to the principle laid down by the right hon. gentleman (Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier) that if necessary county boundaries may be adhered to.
But county boundaries are a secondary consideration to equality of population. The latter principle should as nearly as possible be carried out, and until it is, there will be constant wrangling from one year to another ; and, as I have said before, the greater the injustice perpetrated in any constituency or province, the more disastrous will be the result to the party perpetrating it. All you have to do is to go into the constituency, no matter whether it may have 500 or 600 of a reformed majority, and show the people that, for the purpose of electing a member supporting the right hon. gentleman, this delimitation was made, and the result will be the arousing of the sense of fair play and justice among the electors and the defeat of the party which took this means to maintain itself in power. Into the details of the Bill I shall go later on. What I wish to do now is merely to point out its unfairness. The result, as the hon. gentleman said who spoke in favour of the Bill a moment ago, only affects one province. As regards the provinces of Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Prince. Edward Island and Quebec, the comuSttee were pretty nearly unanimous. What changes were made in those provinces had no political significance. As regards British Columbia the committee was unanimous. In the North-west Territories there was no serious disagreement, and I judge from the statement of the hon. gentlemen supporting the Bill that the changes to be made in Manitoba will make the redistribution of that province acceptable to the whole (House. The whole disagreement is to be found in the province of Ontario, and I consider, from the bottom of my soul, that in that province we have been unfairly dealt with. Instead of giving that province a fair representation, the Hon. Mr. HAGGART.
committee, of which I had the honour of being a member, and of which I felt it my duty to continue being a member to the end, did not deal fairly by that province.

The assumption, then, was that county boundaries must not be disregarded. Our friends on the other side made the welkin ring from one end of Ontario to the other, because we had not adhered to county boundaries. I took the stand then, and I take the stand now, that there was nothing in that contention.
If we were to observe county boundaries in regard to representation in the Dominion parliament, the same county district and county organization would be used for both Dominion and provincial political contests. But, under the system of redistribution in the Dominion, county boundaries are not necessarily recognized, and these local organizations of purely provincial character do not come into play, and the people look upon Dominion politics from a broad, national view-point, and separate them from the polities of the provinces or counties.
That is the line that I took then, and I hold to the same logic to-day-identically.
What is there that comes under the jurisdiction of this House that affects the counties- as affording a reason why a county boundary should of necessity be recognized in a Dominion redistribution measure ? Post offices, lighthouses, railways and canals, weights and measures, and all such matters are under the jurisdiction of the Dominion, but with them county boundaries have nothing whatever to do. So, in these respects there is no necessity for having county boundaries observed. As to the equalization of population :	as far as practicable, it certainly would be advisable that the population should be equalized ; but it is quite evident that the number of the electors in new districts will be greater proportionately than In old settled districts. I have no hesitation in saying that a rural district, especially one covering a large area, is entitled to a representative for a smaller unit of population than a city. This is carried out in the old country, and is also recognized here, as it is in almost every country where reasonable government exists on the basis of representative institutions.

That was not intended at the time of confederation. At the time of the Quebec conference in 1807, delegates attended from Prince Edward Island. In the first place the meeting took place at Charlottetown. The great statesmen of that day who were endeavouring to consolidate the different colonies of the British empire on this continent met at Charlottetown, the capital city of the province, from which I have the honour to come. They assembled there and after discussing fully this question they adjourned to the historical city of Quebec and there we find that they arrived at a conclusion. The late D'Arcy McGee, who was one of the principal gentlemen at that conference, made this remark while the people of Prince Edward Island were insisting on full representation : 'We will take one of our large tugs from the St. Lawrence and tow the little island out of the gulf.' I wish to draw attention to the fact that the people of Prince Edward Island, recognizing the difficulties
of the last century in regard to the representation in parliament in regard to the franchise, were very jealous of surrendering their rights at the time of confederation. They were aware that the great struggle which had taken place for the extension of the franchise, had increased during the past century the rights of the people, aud they were jealous of surrendering any of their rights or independence in entering confederation. To substantiate my view, I want to read a resolution which was passed at a meeting held on the 13th of April last, in the town of Tignish, in which I reside. I call the attention of the Minister of Justice to this resolution. It was moved by Mr. J. H. Bell, formerly a member of this House, seconded by Mr. J. A. Brennan, and is as follows :
Whereas at the conference, in 1864, at Quebec, whilst the delegates from other provinces contended that if Prince Edward Island entered confederation it must do so with a membership in the Commons based on the population, of Quebec and a general unit of representation, on the other .hand our Island delegates insisted that six members-two for each county-would be the only kind of representation that would suit our conditions ; that any number less than six would give this province no sufficient status or influence at Ottawa ; and that if we could not be admitted with that representation we would stay out of the union.
And whereas, in 1873, during the discussion with the delegates of this province of the final terms of confederation the federal government contended that insomuch as our then population of about 95,000 was barely equivalent to five units of representation we were entitled to only a representation of live members ; but our delegates insisted that our representation should be placed on a different footing from that of the other provinces ; and that it should be laid down as a principle applicable to this Island that 95,000 of a population was sufficient to entitle us to a representation of six members.
And whereas the principle for which this province had always contended was finally agreed to by the federal government and embodied in our special terms of union.
And whereas that principle so agreed to rvas not limited in its application to any decade or other period of time but was meant and intended to he absolute and permanent in its operation-so long, at least, as we held 95,000 of a population.
And whereas with that understanding and subject to that agreement, the question of confederation with Canada was submitted to the people of this province at the polls and was approved by the electorate, and the union finally consummated.
And whereas up to the year 1892 this province retained its representation of six on the basis of having continuously a population of 95,000 and upw-ards ; but in that year the federal government unjustly undertook to apply, and did apply, to our conditions the principle of representation which obtained in the other provinces, and so the number of our members was wrongfully reduced from six to five.
And whereas in pursuance of the powers contained in an imperial statute passed in 1871 the parliament of Canada recently added a large

extent of territory to what in 1873 constituted the province of Quebec, thereby increasing the population of that pivotal province, and increasing as well the unit of representation.
And whereas this enlargement of the boundaries of Quebec, taken in connection with making our representation depend on the population of that province will still further operate adversely and unjustly against the retention by us of our former representation.
And whereas, at the present session of the federal parliament, notwithstanding that this province has a population of 95,000 and upwards, it is contemplated to still further reduce our representation from five to four, and Prince County is to be reduced to one-half of the representation it had at confederation-to one-half the number of members it is justly entitled to under the terms of union.
And whereas, under section 52 of the British North America Act, it is provided that the proportionate representation which a province had at confederation should not be disturbed.
Be it therefore resolved that this representative meeting express its emphatic and indignant protest against the action of the federal parliament in 1892 in reducing our representation to five, and against the contemplated action of the federal parliament at its present session of a further reduction to four, such reduction being a manifest breach of faith with the people of this province, and a direct violation of the special terms, as to representation, that were made with us when we entered confederation.
Now, Sir, I desire to dwell at some length upon the phase of the question presented by this resolution, and as it is six o'clock I will resume when the House meets at eight o'clock.

HUGHES (King's. P.E.I.) I have listened with some surprise to the remarks of my hon. friend (Mr. Hackett), in view of the fact that some ten years ago, when the last Redistribution Bill was under consideration, and when the representation of Prince Edward Island was first reduced, my hon. friend and his political associates in Prince Edward Island did not raise a solitary objection. At that time there were two Conservative representatives from the county of King's in this House, and neither of them raised any objection. My hon. friend at that time, though not a member of this House, was an influential man in the riding which he now represents, and took an active part in politics. At that time not a meeting was held in the hon. gentleman's constituency, not a resolution was passed, no objection was raised, no protest was entered against the reduction of the representation of Prince Edward Island. Now, why bring it up at this late date ? In my opinion, the proper time to enter a protest was when the representation was first reduced. But the hon. gentleman's political friends were then in power, and perhaps it was not thought to be good political tactics to bring up the question at that time.
As I listened to the hon. gentleman's remarks this evening, I could not help thinking what an oportunity he lost when he failed to go before the Supreme Court and argue the case of Prince Edward Island when this matter was submitted to it for decision. He made a strong argument here to-night, and it is a pity this argument was not presented when the Supreme Court was considering the case. If there had been any constitutional objection to my hon. friend appearing before the Supreme Court on account of being a layman, I am sure if he had given his views to the counsel who was representing Prince Edward Island, that gentleman would have been very glad to present them before the court. The hon. gentleman says that in 1881 the government of Sir John A. Macdonald allowed Prince Edward Island to retain its original representation, though the population of the province did not entitle it to that representation. The reason of that was, I think, because the census of 1881 was the first Dominion census that was taken after the island entered confederation, and consequently there was no previous census with which to compare that one, so far as Prince Edward Island was concerned. Therefore, no one could tell whether the 20 per cent saving clause would protect the province against any reduction in its representation. That, I think, was the reason why the government of Sir John A. Macdonald at that time did not reduce the representation, at all events, it would be a good and sufficient reason. But in 1891-92, when the next census was taken, the representation of that province was reduced. At that time, I think, Sir John Thompson was leader of the government-if not, he was Minister of Justice-and he declared there was nothing in the constitution to protect the province against a reduction in its

representation. As I have already pointed out, tlie Conservative representatives in this House at that time, the Conservative party and press of Prince Edward Island- everybody, acquiesced in the reduction that then took place. Therefore, I think it is altogether too late for nay bon. friend and his political associates from Prince Edward Island to try to make political capital oult of it at this time. We have to abide by the constitution under which we live.
I regret as much as any man can regret that the delegates at the time the province of Prince Edward Island joined the union overlooked this important points and did not provide against the contingency that has since arisen. I also regret that a reduction has taken place in the representation of the other maritime provinces, because it will weaken the voice of those provinces down by the sea to that extent in the great council of the nation. In view of the fact that the highest constitutional authorities in Canada have declared that the law affords the maritime provinces no protection against a reduction of their representation, that there is nothing in the British North America Act that will preserve their original representation, I believe, however, that if the matter was properly presented to our friends from the other provinces they would agree to a change in the British North America Act providing that the representation of none of the provinces should be reduced beyond the representation they possessed when they originally entered confederation. 1- believe that if the members from the other provinces would agree to that, it could be carried out, and possibly and probably that will be done before the next decennial revision takes place. That is the only way, in my judgment, that this matter can be accomplished. I cannot understand what myl hon. friend had in view in bringing up this question to-night, unless it were to try to make political capital out of it. As I say, we have to abide by the constitution under which we live, and in view of the fact that this question has been argued before the highest court in Canada and decided against us, I am sure my hon. friend has sense enough to know that nothing he could say this evening would affect the issue in any way. He has merely brought up the matter again for the purpose of seeing it ventilated in Prince Edward Island, and giving the Conservative newspapers down there something to talk about, and an occasion to raise some objection to the present administration.

I propose also to present some figures in Illustration of the position I take and to, emphasize the fact that the objections to the action that was taken by the committee are fairly taken. So much then for the scope of the discussion. First of all I wish to find out the principles upon which they proceeded if I can, because I regret to say that neither the Bill nor anything contained in the speech of the right hon. leader of the government (Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurler) in introducing the Bill, gave us any idea of any rule that was to govern the action of the committee further than one proposition which was not in the Bill, but which the right hon. gentleman enunciated in his speech, and that was that county boundaries should be adhered to. That is the principle upon which the division of ridings had been made, and that is the reason why I propose to detain the House for a short time, because I desire to consider this principle.
I will read a couple of extracts from speeches delivered by the right hon. leader

of tlie government in this House. I will first quote with the object of arriving at some conclusion as to how the proceedings of the committee agreed -with the only principle I can find that the right hon. gentleman has laid down since he came into power. In 1899 a Bill was introduced by hon. gentlemen opposite, but it was rejected by the Senate, because of its unconstitutionality on the ground that there being no census in sight at the time, it was not the proper time, according to our constitution, for any such Bill to be passed. However, hon. gentlemen opposite, under the leadership of the right hon. gentleman, passed the Bill. As far as the House of Commons is concerned, or as, far as the authority and jurisdiction of the government went they passed it into law, and I want to quote from it to show the character of the redistribution which was then contemplated. The principles pertinent to the question which were laid down by the right hon. gentleman and subsequently included in the Bill when it was introduced, I will read from 1 Hansard ' of 1899, as follows :
Where, under the foregoing provisions, any county or city is to be divided into more than one electoral district, such divisions shall be made by a board of commissioners, consisting of at least three persons, being judges of the Supreme Court of Judicature for Ontario, who for that purpose shall be appointed by letters patent under the great seal, and who shall divide the city of Toronto and each such county into the number of electoral districts by this Act assigned to them respectively.
The letters patent appointing the commissioners, shall request the commissioners, in making the divisions, to consider the distribution of population according to the last Dominion census, the public convenience, and such divisions as appear to them best calculated to do substantial justice.
These were the principles solemnly laid down and which, in so far as the House of Commons was concerned, became law. They were rejected by the Senate, not on the principle of the Bill, but because the Senate thought it was not in accordance with the British North America Act that a redistribution should take place at any time except following a census. In that view this side of the House concurred. We took the same objection to the Bill. Hon. gentlemen must have been very strong in their views at that time as to these principles. I concur in them to a great extent. I concurred then by a speech which I made, in a redistribution of that sort, as did the Conservative party, and there was a union on that most important principle between both sides of the House for the first time in connection with the question of redistribution. This is one of the most important principles that could be enunciated, and I may here mention while it is in my mind, that I shall have some remarks to offer at a later stage on the general principle connected with these matters. I propose, at a later stage, probably 342
by a motion of which I have given notice, to voice the opinion which I as well as others hold upon this question, but which motion will have to be postponed until a later stage of the proceedings upon this Bill. I say then, that hon. gentlemen must have been very strong in their view upon this question, because they were not satisfied with enunciating these principles in the Bill introduced in 1899. They were not content with the ruling of the Senate, which was quite within their jurisdiction, because, in the following year, 1900, they introduced the same Bill again. It was practically a reprint of the former Bill, and in the most solemn way the right hon. gentleman and his supporters pledged themselves that divisions of counties and divisions of any sort should hereafter be made by a judicial body. That brings me to the attitude of the right hon. gentleman and his government in regard to the principles which they have adopted in the present Bill, and in order that there may be no mistake I will quote an extract from the commencement of the speech of the right hon. gentleman, delivered upon the introduction of that Bill, because I think it is very pertinent for us, in order to understand these things, to know in what way the partition or redistribution of this county that I have objected to was arrived at, and upon what principles. They are not public principles. The majority of the committee must have had some direction or they were left to their own sweet will and it was simply a question for them to decide what course they should pursue. In the commencement of his speech in introducing the Bill, the right hon. gentleman used some words with which I am fully in accord. He said :
What we have in view and what we desire is to introduce a fair measure that will give all the parties an equal measure of justice, freedom and responsibility.
Everybody will concur in that.
The Liberal party has always contended that the redistribution that must follow each decennial census should take place under certain rules, well understood, well defined, and which everybody could understand. These should he the unwritten law of the country, and apply wherever and whenever a redistribution takes place, and should be applied, whichever party is in power.
I fail to discover anything in this Bill which carries out that proposition of the First Minister. The right hon. gentleman was not speaking there of a principle; he was speaking of the rules and regulations which should govern in the creation, divising and delimitation of the constituencies under'the principle on which the redistribution itself: was to be made, and which later on in his speech he laid down to be county boundaries. My right hon. friend in 1899 and 1900 was ready to follow the English plan in redistributing [DOT] the constituencies, but in 1903 he is very far indeed



from adopting the English system. In England they settled the principle of the Bill by a conference, and they referred the delimitation of all the electoral districts to ia non-partisan commission. The light hon. gentleman had the proper idea in 1900 when he made a new departure in connection with these redistribution Acts, but to-day he has lost sight of that guiding principle. The right hon. gentleman on one occasion did embody the right principle in an Act of parliament, and he pressed it through this House at a time, when, according to our view it was not constitutional to pass it. Not only that, but he felt so strongly in favour of this principle that he reaffirmed it in a second Bill, and so far as the right hon. gentleman is concerned if he had the power it would be the law to-day. I do not want any unwritten rules and unwritten laws on matters affecting the status of the political parties. I have not much experience in politics for I am not a politician, although I have for some time represented a constituency in this parliament, but I have learned that we have to be very careful on both sides of the House In giving to our opponents a proper measure of credit and a proper measure of blame. In matters affecting the two parties there should be fixed written rules for our guidance, and there should be rules so plain that every one could understand him. Where are those rules in this Bill ? When I hear gentlemen opposite announce high principles and when I see them fail to carry these principles out, it reminds me of the words of the great poet. Me thinks thou doth protest too much ; and Shakspere knew human nature well. I am afraid that this protesting and this effort on the part of gentlemen opposite to show that their conduct is fair on political matters, conceals a sinister design. While I am not a politician, yet I at once begin to be a little suspicious at this, and I ask myself :	Why all this protesting V The Prime Minister has a very seductive way about him. I never knew any other man who had such a happy way of making you believe that he means one thing when he is going to turn around and do exactly the opposite. The right hon. gentleman explained the Bill that he introduced. As a matter of fact it was no Bill at all. It was nothing but a skeleton stating in the first clause how many members there should be in the House of Commons of Canada, and then there was a blank schedule to be filled up, and when filled up that would be really the Bill. These were the words of the right hon. gentleman :
Now this is the Bill which I intend to move. There is a schedule attached to it. We intend, after it has been debated and read the second time, to refer it to a special committee, composed of seven members, on which the opposition will be represented by three, to be selected by themselves. The object of the committee will be to create the constituencies which will be Hon. Mr. TISDALE.
allowed to elect members of this House. In other words, we do not present to the House to-day a scheme cut and dried which has to be swallowed holus-bolus by our friends and by the opposition whether they like it or not, so we propose to invite our friends now sitting on the opposition benches to meet us in the committee room and there discuss with us, the division of the constituencies and in fact the creation of all constituencies which shall be empowered to elect the members of this House. We propose to do what has been done in England by the government of Mr. Gladstone. We believe that if our friends opposite will meet us in this way, we can prepare a measure which will be at all events fair to all parties. We believe that if they will agree to meet us in committee, to discuss this Bill fairly, without trying to take an undue advantage over each other, we shall be able to present to the House a measure of which every Canadian will have reason to feel proud, a measure which will be free from those contentious elements which characterized former Redistribution Acts which have been passed in the history of the Dominion of Canada. We intend to do this as a basis to be followed not only Upon this occasion but upon all occasions.
Well, the hon. gentleman's principles are not the same to-day as they were in 1899 and 1900. That may he a long time to expect hon. gentlemen opposite to retain the same principles. If I had not some knowledge of their facility in changing their opinions, I confess that I would be very much surprised; but of all changes of opinion on the part of any political party in the history of this country, or the history of the United States or of England, this is perhaps the most 'remarkable. The right hon. gentleman told us that the question of delimitation was the most important part of the Bill, and we are agreed as to that. We accepted the tribunal offered to us; we showed our good faith, and we thought, although with much misgivings, that possibly a fair arrangement could be secured.
It is sufficient for my present purpose to dwell upon one point, upon which I think it is time we heard some explanation, that is the abandonment of the good and just features of the proposals made by the right hon. gentleman in 1899 and 1900, which entitled the right bon. gentleman to considerable credit. We were committed to that proposal, except that, whereas he proposed to name the judges, we suggested that the chief justices should be the parties ex officio. We thought that in that way it would be less personal with the judges than if they were named, and I say that it is a better principle to refer it to the judges, for I am one of those who believe that under certain circumstances judges constitute the best tribunals. I have gone a little out of my way to emphasize this, in order to show * how near we were together on this great and difficult question. My right hon. friend igrew eloquent in his speech in regard to the rules. He would not trust even the judges-and he was right-unless we gave them instructions upon which they were to proceed. Now, when it came to

this occasion, where blood would follow action, it was different. At that time it was academic, because they thought that probably the Senate might see fit to reject that measure, and they would have plenty of time during three or four years to devise a new scheme by the time there was some one to hit. 1 am trying to give some explanation of the conduct of the hon. gentlemen, for this is one of the things with which they are justly chargeable, that they have offered no explanation of their departure from the principles laid down in 1S99 and repeated in 1900 ; the right hon. gentleman in his speech, forgot them completely. He recalled to memory something which he moved in 1892, although the Conservative party at that time did not accept it. He then moved1 to refer, not the division of the constituencies, but the consideration of the principles on which the redistribution was to take place, but, as I say, in 1899 and 1900, he was so earnest to have a fair redistribution that they passed an Act twice *which the Senate disallowed, in which they laid down rules for the guidance of the judges, a fair and independent tribunal to which he proposed to refer this matter. Why, Sir, I felt anything but proud of the right hon. gentleman when he said, after stating his purpose to refer this matter to a committee of the House-a committee on which he was careful to have a majority-that he preferred that committee to the judges of the land. And I want to tell him his faith was well-founded for the purpose intended; he knew what he was about, but I will go into that more fully later. I will show the results of that later on, but in the meantime I am going to show the result in a neighbouring riding to my own. I warn the right hon. gentleman and his colleagues that had it not been for the action of the 'Senate, the very good set of principles for the division of the constituencies twice laid down by a Bill which passed through this House, would be law to-day, and I would like to see them stand up and repeal that law if it had been enacted. They are repealing it in the sight of heaven and of the people of this country ; they are to-day repealing these excellent principles which they are morally, if not, legally, bound to observe, and they are today referring this to a partisan tribunal- for both sides are partisan-and that is not the sort of a tribunal to which a matter of this kind should be sent. I would not vote to place a matter of this kind within the control of a committee of members controlled by a majority of my own party. I would not put them in the position to be suspected, even if they tried to be honest and fair. It it not a proposition that commends itself; it is' a proposition in which hon. gentlemen themselves have no faith. In one way 342i
they have faith in it, but they would not want to refer it to a committee composed of four members from this side of the House and three members from their side. I would not ask any one to trust me in politics unless I could trust him, and I say that this is not a tribunal that will commend itself ; it is not fair to those in the majority if they act straight, and the minority are helpless, because their votes will not count. I say, therefore, it was an unfortunate tribunal, land I regret to have to say-and I am now only applying it to one case-that it has been conclusively shown to any mind that the committee has not acted fairly in a political sense.
