speechtext: May I ask the hon. gentleman a question ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Certainly.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Did not the hon. gentleman say in reference to the proposition he now eulogizes that 'this is a farce, and nothing but a farce ' ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Which is that ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: The reference to the judges and the division of the counties by them.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I said I was in favour of a reference to the judges, but I said that the conditions in the Bill, that you should name what counties should be divided-for you did not pretend to leave it to the tribunal to say what counties should be divided, and you would not allow more than a certain number of counties that were entitled to more than two or three members to be divided-I said that was a farce, because, taking the case of my own riding, if the judges divided fairly on the principles laid down they could not, unless they carved the municipalities, make a fair representation that would not tell in favour of hon. gentlemen opposite.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I understood the hon. gentleman to say now that while he was in favour of sending this matter to the judges, it should be sent with instructions.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Certainly, that was in the Bill, and the instructions were given. If you had applied it to all the counties, there would be a great distinction. You were applying the rule only to the counties you were to name. You did not leave it to be applied to a number of other counties which you did not name, and which you had already fixed so that you could not help winning a majority of them. I am surprised, and I want to say to the hon. Minister of Customs that I am grieved, that now, for the first time in this House or during a long political life on the stump, I have been accused of misrepresenting a matter of this kind. It is the first time that I have ever been accused of misrepresentation.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I did not accuse the hon. gentleman.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
I beg the hon. gentleman's pardon, he certainly did. No other inference could be drawn from his remarks. If I have not correctly interpreted what he said, I will walk out of the House and never appear in it again. There is no charge more pernicious than one which is envolved in words that may be technically construed to mean something else. I wish to say to the hon. gentleman that if I do not press my amendment to-night, it is because I wish to give him another chance to see if he cannot do the fair thing. I know that there is no use trying to convince him at present, because a man convinced against his will is of the same opinion still. But I propose to give him another chance and defer making my motion until the Bill goes through committee, because I would like to see this matter, for the sake of both parties in the country, arranged in such a way that we can get entirely rid of the disagreeable discussions which continually arise in connection with these redistributions. I am firmly convinced that in this particular case, the proper and the fair thing has not been done. Let me take up the city of Brantford. Before this Bill was introduced, two important bodies in that city made representations to this government. One was the city council, which is mixed in politics, and the other was the board of trade, which is also mixed in politics, but the members of which are not elected on political grounds, as the members of city councils frequently are. The resolution of the city council reads as follows :
Therefore, he it resolved that this council Is of the opinion that Brantford city has now reached sufficient importance, both as to population and otherwise to have a representative of its own, and that in the redistribution about to take place, Brantford city be made a constituency for the election of a member of the House of Commons, and that a copy of this resolution be sent by the clerk to Sir Wilfrid Laurier ; Hon. C. Fitzpatrick, Minister of Justice : Hon. William Paterson, Minister of Customs, and Mr. C. B. Heyd, M.P., at Ottawa, at once, so that they may know the wishes of this city before the proposed Redistribution Bill becomes law.
This resolution was carried by nine votes against five. The board of trade about the same time passed the following resolution, proposed by Mr. C. H. Waterous and seconded by Mr. W. George Eliott, and each of these gentlemen bold opposite political; views, Mr. Waterous being a very influential Liberal and Mr. Eliott being equally prominent on the other side :
The following motion was then introduced by Mr. C. H. Waterous, seconded by Mr. W. George Eliott,-
That the board of trade is of the opinion that, in any Redistribution Bill enacted by the Dominion parliament, provision should be made for representation by the city of Brantford, as Hon. Mr. TISDALE.
a separate electoral district, that representations to this effect be forwarded by the president and secretary to the Premier, Sir Wilfrid Laurier ; and that the members of parliament for the county of Brant be requested to urge the adoption of these views by the government and in the House of Commons.
The motion carried.
This motion was carried, I presume, unanimously, as no division Is given. Whatever importance may be attached to these resolutions, I do not think that the views of such important bodies should be utterly set aside. Let me say further, to my hon. friend from Brant (Mr. Heyd) that there is an alternative proposition of which he might have availed himself. It was pointed out to him by the city paper that a riding could have been made of a much better shape than he made of the city, when he insisted upon loading it up with a couple of townships, and that there would be only a difference of twelve in the population. I may say that the majority of the committee refused to be guided by any rules or cardinal principles, and would not commit themselves to any general principle, but sought to take advantage of the circumstance in each case. In the case of Brantford, the hon. member claims that the population of the township of Tuscarora ought to be counted in, although its population consisted of Indians, numbering 3,170, none of whom has a vote. The committee resolved to divide Brant into two ridings-one, the riding of Brantford, which included the city and two townships, and the other, the riding of Brant, which included the balance.
And, as I have said, there is an Indian reservation, the township of Tuscarora, possibly the only one in the older settled parts of Ontario, where there is not a single vote and which has a population of 3,170. I will proceed now, by illustration and figures to show what has happened there, then give the propositions on both sides, then the alternative propositions, and then, possibly, some things incidental to the application. In the first place, I will submit a table showing the municipalities as they are now under the Bill, on the basis of the whole population, including the Indians, for that is what was acted upon by the committee. In the second place, I will give the number of voters by municipalities, and the difference in these cases. The number of voters is pertinent in this case, in view of the considerable element of population that has no vote-people who are simply the wards of the country. These people have a township of their own, governed under special regulations. And while, under a legal technicality, you may load these people on to one constituency, counting them as a part of the population, simply because the census showed so many individuals in the township, that is certainly not carrying out the spirit of the law. In the third place I will show what has been called the city plan, the one that proposes that the city of

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I think there are about 18,000 Indians in the province of Ontario. Does the hon. gentleman want those all to be left out, and thereby reduce the representation of Ontario in this House ?

speechtext: Then why interrupt me 7

speechtext: The hon. gentleman is quite right in what he says about that, but he would have to divide the city in the way he is stating.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
I would not have to divide the city. I would allow the constituency to pass over the river. That would be a very small difficulty because there is a bridge and the people would come across. No, I do not propose to divide the city. I would take the city with that part of the township which is surrounding it and we will have the advantage of having a compact riding lying out to the east side of Brantford; whereas, hon. gentlemen take the west part of the township of Brantford and the township of Oakland and place them absolutely between the big township of Burford and the other parts of the riding of Brant as the Bill constitutes it, so that they surround the whole riding of Brantford by the bounds of the county of Brant and the big township of Burford. That is somthing I do not think there is any necessity for. To make it clear and to be understood by the committee I have a little plan and I will show it to the committee. These dark lines represent the divisions of the municipalities. This is the line of the Grand river. The black part includes the city of Brantford. I had ' Brantford ' riding put in black because the people there are rather sad and are weeping at the way they are being treated. I had ' Brant ' riding put in red, because the faithful are jubilant. They have these red men amongst them, and they ought to	be red.
There is the township of Tuscarora, with 3,170 Indians, and not a vote. My hon. friend is not ashamed to put them in and to count them as forming part of the riding of ' Brant,' but he is unfair enough not to allow them to vote. This is pretty hard on poor Lo and it is a very low thing to do in some ways. We do not admire this. Here is the Grand river and here is the cit^y of Brantford. Here is the five cent piece as compared with the big dollar across the river. Here are the two townships which have been put into the electoral district of Brantford and the rest of this space includes this great big township which is sandwiched in between, so that the electors cannot get to the polls to vote unless they go through this township.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Just as it was in North Wentworth in 1882.

When that time comes, I will no longer be the representative of South Brant. No one can have a greater interest than I have in seeing that the work of the redistribution in the county I represent shall be done properly and to the satisfaction of a majority of tiie people. That is my only object. One of the reasons that have been assigned as proper to guide us, reasons which we should take into account, is the electoral lists. That is an entirely new argument made for the occasion. The law says they are to take the population into account and that only and that is the only proper plan. In doing that we are conforming to the law as well as to morality and justice.
Some aspersions have been cast because tiie Indians have no votes. I can assure my hon. friend that I am not to blame for that; I am quite willing that the Indians shall have votes and quite satisfied that if they now had the opportunity to cast their votes once more, the Liberal representative of South Brant would have, instead of a majority of 91. a majority of 191, because they have had six more years of experience of what it is to live under a progressive and wise government.
There are two things which our friends have forgotten, that South Brant has been twice gerrymandered by the Conservative party and the people of that riding do not propose that that shall be done a third time. Because While they had large majorities in

this House they dealt unjustly with South Brant, that is no reason why with a majority of fifty Liberals in the House we should allow them to do it once more. I propose that after twenty years South Brant shall be treated justly, and there is sufficient sentiment of justice in this House at the present time to give that justice and that is all we want. Now what are the actual conditions ? The constituency of South Brant has been composed from time immemorial of the city of Brantford, the township of West Brantford, the township of Oaklands, and the township of Burford. For the last fifty years this constituted South Brant, and the balance of the county was North Brant. That lasted until 1880, when for certain purposes Oakland and Burford were taken out of South Brant and put into Oxford and South Brant was reconstituted. I could tell you the reasons why the reconstitution was made, and may do so later on.

I can do it now just as well as another time, but I did not want to enter into a political discussion ip connection with this matter. But my hon. friend opposite from Hatton (Mr. Henderson) said to-day that he was not aware that any particular political advantage had been sought in the redistribution of 1880 and 1890. I have a letter which I think I ought to read to show you exactly how the redistribution was effected some twenty years ago. This letter was read in the House once before, but it may be as well to read it again, because there are many members here who do not know just how the trick was done in 18S2. A gentleman by the name of Hague, over his own signature, who was editor of the ' Journal of Commerce,' wrote as follows :	,
On the 15th of September, 1881, I received a note from a member of the Senate, who represented the government of Sir John Macdonald in Toronto, asking me to call upon him at a certain hour. I was informed that in compliance with the constitution the government proposed to rearrange the constituencies of Ontario.
I was informed that what the government wished to effect was a rearrangement of the electoral districts, so far as possible recognizing a common unit of representation. This, however, was to be made sufficiently elastic to allow the grouping of different sections of the districts so as to detach Conservative voters from places where they were in excess of the needs for a majority, and the attachment of such voters to districts where the new accession would turn the scale at an election in favour of a Conservative candidate where a Liberal one had hitherto been returned. Electoral districts which were hopelessly Liberal were, if possible, to be abolished, or the constituencies so arranged as to put the Liberal voters all together in one district, especially where they could be drawn away from a district where they menaced the Conservative candidate. The process was afterwards called ' hiving,' which is quite appropriate, though -while the w-ork was being done for the Act of 1882 this word was never used.
speakername: Mr.  C. B. HE YD@South Brant

After making a colossal chart I took each electoral district and its surroundings in hand and wrote upon each the number polled for each party at the two previous elections, the total number of electors, with the majority in each case. I coloured each district so as to show at a glance its political complexion.
I then made a thorough study of the official returns of the two last elections, and took out hundreds of statistics for comparison and readjustment. Some of the districts were most difficult to alter so as to secure the results desired. It was said the configuration of some of those represented nothing on earth, in the heavens, or the waters under the heavens. Quite true, they simply represented an effort to fix the boundaries of electoral districts according to two rules: first, on the principle of equal representation to equal numbers of voters: second, on the principle that electoral districts should be arranged to serve the interests of the party in power when they are rearranged. These rules do not work well together, hence the highly eccentric shapes of some of the districts on the chart I have constructed. When nearly complete it was taken down to Ottawa.
I was assigned to a room close to that of the Minister of the Interior. Into that room I was instructed to prohibit the entrance of any one, even of a cabinet minister, unless brought in by the senator. I remember the pretty rage of one minister to whom I refused admission. One day the hon. Mr. Aikens, the Minister of Inland Revenue, came in and saw the chart, upon which he made no comment. His silence elicited the remark : ' Why, Aikens, I am surprised at a strait-laced fellow like you being in such company,' to which Mr. Aikens gave his usual placid smiie. One by one several members were consulted as to the changes made in their districts, amongst others being the late J. C. Rykert, Col. O'Brien and Mr. Mackenzie Bowell. The latter made a little fuss over some feature, but it passed off. When the final touch was put to my chart it was shown to Sir John Macdonald. After closely examining the work done on the boundaries, the statistics written on the face of the map and the schedule I wrote on its side, showing the result of the changes, Sir John exclaimed :	' That takes a great load off my
shoulders.' The Gerrymander Act, as it was called, was simply the chart I had constructed, expressed in legal language. The changes were estimated to have given an absolute gain to the Conservative party of four seats, and a better fighting chance in a number of others.
In the department is a large map, measuring about six by ten feet, and representing the province of Ontario and the Quebec counties of Ottawa and Pontiac. The map itself is a well-finished one, prepared by the draughtsman of the Post Office Department in 1891, and representing the counties as they exist municipally. Over this are carefully drawn the lines of the constituencies as gerrymandered by the Act of 1882. The work is finished with a nicety of detail. Each township, town and village is there, with the voting strength of the two parties marked in blue characters. The available vote and the actual vote polled are each marked. Then follows the Conservative vote, marked (c), and the Reform vote, marked (r). Altogether the chart is a most ingeniously contrived and neatly executed piece of political machinery, evidently designed for use in the gerrymander of 1892, when an attempt was made to make the work of the sweeping gerrymander of 1882 more complete by calling into requisition the surgical

knife to supplement the axe used in hacking to pieces the county organizations, in order to stifle the electoral and ' hive the Grits.'
This is the letter written by the man who did the job. Let me just give a specimen of how the thing worked out in actual practice. The south riding of Brant was constituted by the city of Brantford, the township of Burford, the township of Brantford and the township of Oaklands, and in the elections of 1878 the Liberal candidate got 1,496 and the Conservative 1,298, giving a Liberal majority of 198. That toeing the case, this gentleman, under the direction of his employers, proposed the following changes : The township of Burford gave a Liberal majority of 118 and Oak-lands a Liberal majority of 94. Those two were taken out of the south riding of Brant and put into the south riding of Oxford. We will hive that many Grits. We will put into South Brant ' the township of Onondaga, which gave us a Conservative majority of 40. We will take in the town of Paris, which gave a Liberal majority of 24, and leave in the township of Brantford, which gave a Liberal majority of 118, and the result will be that the next election will give, on that basis, a Conservative majority of 43, and William Paterson will lose the seat. But the thing did not pan out right. The people were disgusted at the unfairness of the redistribution, and Mr. Paterson was elected by 117 votes.
Now, take the county of Wentworth. That is an interesting county, because it operates on South and North Brant. South Wentworth, in 1878, elected Rymal by a majority of 74. Hon. gentlemen opposite wanted to have the Grits in North Brant, so they took Ancasber from South Wentworth, with the Liberal vote of 484 and a Conservative vote of 223, and put it into North Brant, which left 685 Liberals and 878 Tories. They took out of Lincoln Grimsby with a Liberal vote of 344 and a Conservative vote of 271, which left 1,029 Liberals and 1,149 Conservatives, or 120 in favour of tbe Conservative party. But the expectations of the Tory party were again disappointed, and Springer was elected by a majority of 48. But this shows the spirit with which our friends on the other side, the hon. gentlemen who are now so fair, approached these things. They approached it, as my hon. friend says, with a hatchet in 1882 and with a scalping knife in 1892. Now. what effect would that have on North Brant ? That left us the township of East Brantford, which my hon. friend would like to attach to Brantford, and which I would like very much to have. It left South Dumfries, which gave a Liberal majority of 160. and East Brantford, with a Liberal majority of 671 in North Brant, and that is all they left. They took the Conservative parts out and put them in South Brant, where they might do some good. They took Ancaster from Wentworth, with a Liberal majority of 261, and Blenheim out of Oxford, with a Liberal majority of 224. and constituted the Liberal hive of North Brant, with a majority of 712. But again the Tory expectations were deceived, because Somerville was elected by a majority of 951. These are two fair cases of attempting to .influence the constituencies of South Wentworth and South Brant by taking Tories out of North Brant and putting them into South Brant and hiving the Liberals . in North Brant by making four Liberal townships constitute that riding. This was what took place in 1882. And they expect to repeat that here in 1903. They think the Conservatives in Brantford should dictate to the Liberal party bow South Brant shall be reorganized. We have a majority in the city of Brantford. We have a majority in the township of Brantford. We have a majority in Oakland. And we do not propose to allow the arranging of the constituency to be dictated by Tories. For twenty years they politically ruled that roost. But this time the majority of Brant are going to have their own way. not the minority. We propose, what ? To restore conditions as they were long before confederation, to have them as they are for the local legislature, to have them as they ought to be and as the people would like to have them. But, much to my regret, Burford is compelled to go into North Brant to equalize the population.

speechtext:
For twenty years these townships wanted to come back to the constituency of South Brant. For twenty years they have been connected with Oxford, with which they had no business or municipal relation, not nearly the same close relations which they have with the city of Brantford. They have wanted to come back, and we have brought them back to the county of Brant. But, owing to the growth of Brantford city, Burford is obliged to go into the constituency of Brant, while Oakland, in order to establish an equilibrium, goes into Brantford. West Brantford has been, for fifty years, a portion of South Brant. We still propose to bold it. Nature has provided a line of demarcation between North and South Brant by a river which it is difficult to cross. Between Paris and Brantford, a distance of eight miles, there is no way to get across. West Brantford and Oakland do all their trading with Brantford city. For fifty years they have been interested in the political welfare of Brantford,

and we want to take them into Brantford again, and they want to come. Therefore, I say, in restoring conditions as they existed before confederation, in meeting the wishes of the people who live there, and in doing an act of justice, we cannot he charged with doing anything that we should he particularly ashamed of. I feel proud of it, because it is right. It is founded on the principles of justice, convenience and deference to the wishes of the people. What more do we want ? It is right because it gives a fair division of the population. It gives the constituency of Brantford 19,867, and the constituency of Brant 18,273. But, according to the plans proposed by our hon. friends opposite there would be a disparity of over 4,000 instead of 1,900. Why should a city of 16,900 population have a representative, while it takes 22,000 in a rural constituency for one representative. Why should 16 men in the city of Brantford have as much voting power as 22 men in the county? Throughout this redistribution, the principle has been recognized that the rural constituency would have the preference. The city of Brantford, if hon. gentlemen opposite were allowed to have their way, would be the smallest city constituency in the Dominion of Canada, with only 16,900 people. Brantford does not want that. The Conservative city council-tire majority of them-do. Certain members of the board of trade wanted it because it would give the constituency of South Brant the name of Brantford. But, so long as that namie appears the board of trade are satisfied. They did not realize the political significance of what was going on. The Tory wire-pullers who introduced the resolutions in the city council of Brantford, and also in the board of trade, knew what they were about; but the members of thq board of trade, not seeing any political significance in the matter, and desiring that the constituency should be called Brantford, which would advertise our constituency throughout the country, some few of them favoured it. But I am quite satisfied that if the board of trade were polled, eight out of ten of the members would vote for the present condition. For the Liberals outnumber the Conservatives on the board of trade By about eight to two. We Liberals are the people of South Brant. We run most of the big factories of South Brant. We employ most of the labour of South Brant. We make the wheels of commerce go in South Brant. We do not propose that South Brant shall be run by the Tory minority.

Well, one for Kingston and Portsmouth with 19,788, and they want to give Brantford one for 16,619. Now, that is an extraordinary liberal proposition, and that shows the confidence they have in the intelligence of the city of Brantford, and they manifest it in sending me here to look after their interests. They knew if they had me here they could trust their affairs in my hands, and that I would not allow Tory city councils or Tory schemers in the board of trade to manipulate the south riding of Brantford. I have every confidence that, should it be my lot once more to appear before them. I will justify this redistribution to the satisfaction of a large majority of people of Brantford. We are not trying to do anything that is unjust. We are not trying to get any political advantage in any form or manner. My hon. friend misrepresents the actual condition of affairs. The township of West Brantford has always been a portion of South Brant, and it gave a Liberal majority of 142. The only new addition we have is the township of Oakland, that cannot possibly belong to any other constituency. I have too high an opinion of the good sense of my hon. friend from South Norfolk to believe that if he were in my place he would not do exactly what I am doing, hanging on to old friends who have stood by you in days gone by, and trying to get back new ones that have been stolen from you by hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House. I am not afraid to meet the people of South Brant. My hon. friend from North Wentworth and Brant (Hon. Sir. Paterson) and I will have to meet the constituency of Brant, and he is as proud of this Bill as 1 am ; and if he can satisfy the people of Brant and I can satisfy the people

of Brantford, and between tbe two of us we can satisfy the people of Brant county, surely no one here who is not so particularly interested, has a right to say nay. If Brant and Brantford constituencies are satisfied with the manner in which my hon. friend and I recommended this division, I do not see that anybody heed complain. If we are making such a fatal blunder that we ought to be ashamed, our errors will be visited upon our own heads. Now, my hon. friend and I are too shrewd to be caught in any such trap, we are too shrewd to try anything unjust, because we know that the people of Brantford and of Brant won't stand anything of that kind. When it was attempted by our Tory friends in 1881, the people of South Brant refused to accept the bait. In 1890 'when they found they were not successful, and they tacked on the Indian constituency of Tuscarora and gave the Indians votes with the expectation that they would wipe out my hon. friend, they were again unsuccessful. We are not going to repeat anything that is unjust. What my hon. friend and I want is absolute justice, something which the people will be satisfied with, and that is the thing we have recommended to the committee. It is a scheme that commends itself to the reasonable Conservatives in the city of Brantford, Nobody objects there but the wire pullers, and they think that if they succeeded in getting a representative for the city of Brantford they would have a better chance to defeat the Liberal representative. Now, what was the result at the last election ? The Liberal majority in the city of Brantford was 65. That iS why they wanted the city of Brantford to have one representative, for it is easier to win the city of Brantford against a majority of 65 than it would be if the township of Brantford was attached, that gave 142 Liberal majority. That was attached in 1896, and in 1900, and has been for fifty years, and will continue to be if I have any influence in this House. What we have done is to take Oakland out of Oxford where it was unjustly put twenty years ago, and bring it back, and in doing that we have been animated by the principles of justice, we have sought the convenience of the people, we have'consulted their wishes, and in recommending what we did we satisfied ourselves and our constituents. This matter, I suppose, will come up in the schedule, but if I speak upon it now it will not be necessary to repeat myself then. I take pleasure in pointing to the division of Brant, because I see
in the report of the majority of the committee that the division has been made with a fairness that gives me confidence that the other divisions are made with equal fairness. The old county of Brant consisted of the north and south ridings-I am speaking prior to the gerrymander of 1882- as constituted in 1853, when the county was formed. The south riding of Brant at that time consisted of the town of Brantford, the town of Burford, the township of Oakland, the half township of Brantford south and west of the river, and the township of Tuscarora. The north riding of Brant consisted of the township of South Dumfries, the township of Onondaga, the half township of Brantford north and east of the Grand river, and the town of Paris. So it remained from 1853, at the time the county was formed, down to 1882, when the gerrymander was perpetrated by the party of hon. gentlemen opposite. They took the township of Burford and Oakland, which 9ad been since 1853 in the south riding of Brant, and placed them in the south riding of the county of Oxford, there being over 200 of a Liberal majority in the two townships, and placed them in the south riding of Oxford where there was already a Liberal majority of 600. Now this committee are bringing back the principle laid down by the Prime Minister so far as they could, bringing back the principle of county boundaries which Sir John A. Macdonald in 1871 recognized. In returning to that principle there is no doubt that some advantages will result, provided the votes are polled as they have been, some results will inure to the benefit of the Liberal party. But that is not a gerrymander on the part of the Liberals now, that is an undoing of a gerrymander, and bringing us back to where we were before. Now, that is with reference to the county of Brant. What did they do when they came within the lines ? They knew what it was when it was divided as a county, and they recognized the fact that regard must be had to population, when it could be done. They found that the city of Brantford had increased very largely in population, much faster than the adjoining county. What did they do then ? In restoring county boundaries they found, through the growth of the city, the only way in which the population could be equalized would be by taking the townships of Burford and Tuscarora, which hitherto have been in South Brant, and attaching them to North Brant. They did not take them out of the county, they simply took them from one riding to the other, with the result that they just about equalized the ridings. South Brant as at present constituted under the report of this committee, will be composed of the city of Brantford, part of the township of Brantford, south and west of the river, and the township of Oakland-all, remember, were in South Brant and had been since 1853. They are just

leaving enough of old South Brant and taking away from South Brant sufficient territory to add to North Brant to equalize the population.

Now, they are proposing to cut out one member and only give Bruce two members which I think is entirely wrong taking into consideration the representation that is given to other constituencies with a less population. Now, the division line as it was previous to the gerrymander or redistribution of 1882 is the line which I wish to have restored at the present time. The proposed redistribution adds to my constituency of East Bruce no less than five Reform municipalities. The riding as at present constituted is a very close one. In 1887 I was brought out as a hopeless victim. There was no chance for me in the election in East Bruce. However, I buckled on my armour and I succeeded in converting an adverse majority of 185 into a favourable majority of 373. Should I desire, notwithstanding the proposed redistribution, to be a candidate for South Bruce at the next election, and not-

withstanding the political complexion of that riding, I think I would be able to succeed just as well as I did in East Bruce in 1887. I do not rely very much upon the political complexion of the riding. I always think that a man who has a fairly good reputation for honesty and integrity and who, when appealing to the people, shows that there is merit in the cause which he advocates will get the majority of the votes of the constituency especially in Bruce, because the electors there are a very intelligent class of people. This remark applies to a great many Liberals in that constituency, and I want to say that if I could not get a great many Liberal votes in East Bruce I could not be elected to represent East Bruce in this House. I owe my election largely to the support which I have received from the Reformers of East Bruce. I rose for the purpose of appealing to the right hon. leader of the government, who, when he submitted the proposal to appoint this conference to redistribute the constituencies throughout the length and breadth of the Dominion he made I thought a fair proposition. He followed this by saying that this appeared iu the ' Herald,' and afterwards, published in the ' Globe,' and he assumed if it were not correct libel suits would have followed. It does not follow because incorrect articles which appear in party newspapers, are not followed by libel suits that they are correct. We know as a fact, that in many cases, although members of parliament know that articles are published which are entirely inaccurate they neither take the trouble to refute them nor to commence libel suits. The hon. gentleman went on and gave us a little piece of information in the letter which he read. This individual, whoever he was, says :
I was assigned to a room close to that of the Minister of the Interior. Into that room I was instructed to prohibit the entrance of any one, even of a cabinet minister, unless brought in by the senator. I remember the petty rage of one minister to whom I refused admission. One day the hon. Mr. Aifcens, the Minister of Inland Revenue, came in and saw the chart, upon which he made no comment. His silence elicited the remark : ' Why, Aikens, I am surprised at a strait-laced fellow like you being in such company,' to which Mr. Aikens gave his usual placid smile. One by one several members were consulted as to the charges made in their districts, amongst others being the late J. C. Rykert, Colonel O'Brien and Mr. Mackenzie Bowell. The latter made a little fuss over some feature, but it passed off.
Now as one who was present at the time, and who happens to know something about this matter, I simply want to say that if the balance of this communication is no more nearly correct than what 1 have read, the whole thing is simply trash. The chart remained there in the room for any one to see, during the whole time the redistribution was being considered, in 1882. In 1892

a similar chart was put up in room 16, and I have no doubt it was seen by dozens of Liberal members of the House, because some of them looked at it with myself. Sir Mackenzie Bowell, the gentleman who is said to have made the complaint, was the party who was in charge of the work, and who was looking after it. This shows the absurdity and the untruthfulness of his statement, and how little value can be placed upon the article which is produced here to-night as evidence that there was but one aim and view at that time. 1 say that in neither case was the chart kept secret ; it was simply a map with the ridings as they then existed shown in one colour, and with the ridings as they were proposed shown in another colour. It appears that there is a question between the Finance Department and the Auditor General's department, under which the Auditor General is unable to authorize certain cheques or to make application to the minister for certain cheques. He is not furnished with the usual statements, and it is supposed that these statements are intercepted in some quarter. I would like to ask the Minister of Finance for an explanation of what the difficulty is and why there would be any such difficulty.

maintopic: TREASURY BOARD AND AUDITOR GENERAL-PAYMENT OF MEMBERS.
speechtext: I see no reason in the world why the difficulty should exist, but the difficulty exists all the same. The Treasury Board, in the exercise of what they believe to he their proper function, made certain regulations regarding the manner in which the public accounts should be managed, having special regard to a difficulty which occurred some time ago. The Auditor General has taken exception to these regulations. The Department of Justice have advised that the regulations of the Treasury Board are entirely proper and regular, and within the statute. That is the position. It may be necessary to have legislation. At jn'e-sent I am not able to tell my hon. friend (Mr. Barker) more than this.

maintopic: TREASURY BOARD AND AUDITOR GENERAL-PAYMENT OF MEMBERS.

speechtext:
I think that Brantford ought to stand and that Brant ought to carry. I will ask my hon. friend from South Norfolk (Hon. Mr. Tisdale) to read the section which we have before us :
The county of Brant, exclusive of the electoral district of Brantford as hereinafter defined.
Shall return one member. It is well understood that the two sides have agreed that the county of Brant should have two members. The county of Brant constitutes the electoral district except the part which is to constitute the electoral district of Brantford. The view of the majority was that the electoral district of the city of Brantford should be composed of the city of Brantford, the township of Oakland and part of the township of Brantford. If this view is confirmed the county of Brant will, be composed of everything except the city of Brantford, the township of Oakland, and part of the township of Brantford. If, on the other hand, the views of the minority prevail, and the electoral district of Brantford is restricted to the city of Brantford, then the electoral district of the county of Brant will be composed of the whole county of Brant, less the city of Brantford. There can be no objection that I can see to adopting this clause at the present time.	.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I understand that the clause says there shall be two ridings, and my motion will affect both. My motion provides for the alternative proposition that I argued in favour of last night. My motion will be to amend the clause by taking a part of each riding, and therefore, if it is made clear that this will not be out of order I have no objection to this step being taken, and to making the motion at a later stage.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: My hon. friend will not be out of order. What I understand my hon. friend wants is to have the county of Brant divided into two ridings. We do not, however, agree as to the manner of forming these ridings. When we come to the city of Brantford, then, my hon. friend will be able to have an opportunity of moving the motion that he wants to move.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
I want some information before we proceed further as to what principle governed this committee. The right
hon. leader of the government in answer to a question yesterday said :
It is impossible in a country like this with its enormous territory and with its sparse population to give an urban population the same rate of representation as is given to a rural population.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Brant is an old, well settled and compact county territorially. Brant, with a population of 38,140, including Brantford, is given two members, while the district of Haliburton and the county of Victoria, which have a population of 38,511, are only given one member. May I ask for an explanation respecting this principle ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: The explanation is quite easy. The committee to which the duty was assigned of drafting a schedule have reported unanimously that the county of Brant should be represented by two members.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Were they unanimous ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: They were unanimous in so far as the county of Brant should be represented by two members. They differed as to the distribution of those two members within that territory.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: That is not an answer. We look to the right hon. leader of the government, in view of the splendid statement he made in introducing this measure, to see that justice shall be done. If the principle is to prevail that urban constituencies are not to have the same measure of representation according to population as sparsely settled parts of the province, upon what principle will the right hon. gentleman support the report of the committee which gives the county of Brant, including Brantford, with 38.140 souls, two representatives, while the sparsely settled district of North Victoria, with a larger population, will only have one representative in this House ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: The only answer I can give to my hon. friend is that it is impossible in these matters to have things settled according to compass absolutely. You must give and take. The committee have made a unanimous report upon one point, and if they have met the requirements in that one point, we are not disposed to disturb the recommendation.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
Then, we are not to pay strict attention to the accuracy of this statement :	*
It is impossible in a country like this with its enormous territory and with its sparse population to give an urban population the same rate of representation as is given to a rural population.*
The district of Haliburton is an immense district, sparsely settled, and the northern

part of Victoria is in the same position. These two, Victoria and Haliburton, have a larger population than that which exists in the compact, well settled county of Brant and the city of Brantford, yet they are only given one representative, while this smaller district territorially, and with less population, is given two members.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: In saying that I have no objection to this stage being taken, I do not want it to be understood that I consent to the principle, but I do not propose to divide the committee on every principle I may object to. I have no objection if it is understood that I shall have an opportunity of introducing my motion, but I do not want it to be understood that I am consenting to any of these provisions by doing so.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
The hon. Prime Minister has entirely overlooked the essence of the question raised by the hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Clarke). I quite understand that it was agreed that Brant should have two representatives. That I think is quite correct and that conclusion was arrived at, as I understand, by adopting a unit of representation for the whole province of something exceeding 36,000. The population of Brant was larger than that and therefore that county was entitled to two representatives. But I do not agree that Haliburton and Victoria should have only one. The right hon. the Prime Minister has made this Bill his own, he has become responsible for every feature bad and good in it.
The P1UME MINISTER, Hear, hear.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: For the simple reason that it was agreed that the smaller one was to have two.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Then it follows reasonably that the larger one should certainly have two. The hon. gentleman could ascertain the reason if he turned to the hon. gentleman to his right (Mr. Hyman) who is anxious that the county of Middlesex shall have three representatives although there are a half dozen other counties much larger.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: My hon. friend (Mr. Clancy) does not seem to reflect how illogical he .is. We are dealing with the county of Brant and I would ask him whe-there he finds fault or not with Brant having two members.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: No, Brant is entitled to two members.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: When we come to Haliburton we will discuss Haliburton.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: The right hon. gentleman has no right to insist on a smaller county being given the two members until he is prepared to take the responsibility of stating now, even before we reach that county, why the larger counties are not given two members.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: My hon. friend (Mr. Clancy) is more and more illogical. He agrees to Brant having two members. Very good ; we are dealing with Brant, in debate he accepts the division that is proposed for the county, and what objection has he to saying so in the Bill V If he says so in debate why not in the Bill ? My hon. friend says : But Haliburton has one member and should have two, and Middlesex has three and should have only two. When we come to these counties we will discuss the objections of my hon. friend but I do not understand what my hon. friend means when he says that Brant should have two members, but that we should not put it in the Bill. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Clancy) should be as good ns his word and his reasoning; since he says that Brant should have two I simply want his word to be put upon the Bill.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: We will see who is illogical in this case. Does the right hon. gentleman think, leaving aside any question of whether it is fair politically, that there is any reason why Brant should have two members-although according to the unit of population it is entitled to them-and a larger county should have only one.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: What larger county ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I am not asking the hon. gentleman.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I asked the hon. gentleman a civil question

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: and of course he can decline to answer It. I asked to what larger county he referred.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: The county of Victoria and Haliburton.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I do not suppose that any member of this House understands the situation better than my hon. friend (Mr. Clancy) cr knows better than he does that there is no such thing as a county of Victoria and Haliburton. Haliburton is a provisional district in the province of Ontario with a population of something between 6,000 and 7,000. As it was not entitled to a member, it was necessary that the people in that district should be given an opportunity to exercise their franchise in connection with some other district. When we come to that, as the Prime .Minister has rightly said, we can discuss it. The proposition of some members of the committee was to unite this with another adjoining county which would leave the population smaller. It was thought by others, and especially by the member for Victoria, who is familiar with the district, that it would be better on account of the judicial connection and on account of the roads and physical conditions to unite it in this way even if the population was larger. He, of course, with the others, argued that we should join these two counties together and give them two representatives. That would be an injustice to some other places because the principle of county lines was adhered to almost absolutely.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Only when it suited a party purpose.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
There never was an exception made except by the unanimous agreement of the committee. My hon. friend has no right to say 'when it suited any party purpose.' I do not intend to waste much time over a discussion of this Bill, although I am most anxious to make any explanation or give any information. The people living in these counties and districts will know whether or not there is any foundation for the statement that an injustice has been done. I am willing to leave it to them. They did resent the injustice of the gerrymander on a previous occasion and I am satisfied, after dealing with this matter in a fair and just way, to leave it to the people in the district and not leave it to the slight statements made here as to great and flagrant injustice. There is no foundation for any such statement and I am perfectly willing to leave the decision to the people of these counties and districts. The people who live in these districts and know the conditions, cannot be misled by misrepresentation and they know whether the division now proposed is according to their preference. When we come to these counties if it is the feeling of a majority that a change should be made the committee is not bound to adhere to the
recommendations made. The special committee only say that after hearing the statements of the hon. gentlemen representing these constituencies, the recommendations they have made appear to them to be the best under all the conditions. You cannot perhaps lay down any rule that will govern under all conditions and circumstances, but I do say that we endeavoured throughout to do what we considered was fair and just and it 'will rest on the hon. gentleman to show to the country that it was not-and to show it not by exaggerated statements or wild adjectives.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Is there anything wild in the statement as to the population of Victoria and Haliburton ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I say it was a misstatement to speak of the county of Victoria and Haliburton, there is no such thing.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Is not there a provisional district of Haliburton and a county of Victoria ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: There is no such thing as a municipal county of Victoria and Haliburton, and it was only with municipal counties that we were dealing.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: That will not do.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I say the Act provides only for municipal counties, not for provisional counties. That is clear and every layman knows that is exactly the class of county we are dealing with and I say it is a misrepresentation when we are dealing with this question to refer to it as ' the county of Victoria and Haliburton.' These two districts constitute a judicial county, and it is no more proper to refer to them as a municipal county than it would be to refer to the county of Toronto and York, which, I understand, form a judicial county.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Then why does the hon. gentleman say in the schedule : * for municipal and judicial purposes ' ?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: We are making no progress at all. The question, really before the committee, and the one to which I must urge the committee to confine itself, is whether the county of Brant is properly divided.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: No.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
What is under discussion is this subclause of the schedule :
The county of Brant, exclusive of the electoral district of Brantford as hereinafter defined.	[DOT]
The others were passed, and no objection was taken until I reached the first subsection. That is what is under consideration, and the discussion of the division outside of the county of Brant I rule out of order.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Will you allow me to remind you that I raised the point that we were going beyond what we should-that there was a difference in meaning between judicial districts and municipal districts, and that we were confined to what were municipal districts.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Order. After I read the first subsection, the acting leader of the opposition asked me if I had read the first part of it. I said that I had. It was after that, that you drew the attention of the committee to that point.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: You never made the slightest pause from the time you started to read that schedule until you got down to section 1; and as the district of Victoria and Haliburton has been brought up to-day, I would point out

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: That is my ruling, and there is only one way of getting over it, that is by appealing from my decision.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I must apologize if I have violated the rules in any way. I was just following the remarks of my kon. friend, which I thought at the time were in order.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I did not call to order any person particularly, but I wish to direct the attention of the committee to the subject that is really under discussion. When I read the section, I understood the Premier to state that we would confine ourselves to each subsection.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Pardon me. You read the counties down to the word ' defined ' in section 1. The question was not put, because I asked the Prime Minister for some explanation of this item. I appeal to the Prime Minister if in his opinion that introduction has been carried. The word ' carried ' has not been pronounced in the House this morning.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I want to ask the Prime Minister

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: No, this point must be settled.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: A solemn farce. It is well that we should understand whether we are precluded absolutely from any discussion except on the sub-item which we are dealing with at the moment.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: 1 should be sorry if this Bill, which is of so much importance, should be treated as a farce. I think it is not only a solemn but a very important duty that we are discharging. If my hon. friend calls it a farce. I do not agree with him. This duty has to be performed by somebody. At present it has to be performed by the House of Commons, and if it is a farce, it must be made a farce by the man who treats it as such.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Not at all. It is made a farce by the means you propose.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: The Troceed-ing is a very solemn one. I stated a moment ago that section 2 had been reserved, not having been agreed to. I stated further that I thought that we should take up the schedule item by item, that we should adopt the items so far as we could agree, that those on which we could not agree should be reserved, and the whole section should not be understood as accepted until it should be considered. The chairman has stated, and I think quite rightly, that we should confine our attention to the item of the schedule we are now discussing-the county of Brant. Both parties are agreed, I think, that that county should have two members.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I object to the clause being passed pro forma unless we have some explanation from the right hon. gentleman why the rule has been adopted to give a small, compact, thickly populated district two members, and a large sparsely settled county one member.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I want to ask my hon. friend, is he for or against the county of Brant having two members '!

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I will not answer that question until I get an answer to the other.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: My hon. friend will not answer that question ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
Not at present.
Mr. CLANCY'. I rise to a point of order. I want to know if there has been an understanding to justify the ruling you are making. We are discussing clause 1, and I understand your ruling to be that we must take up each separate county by itself, precluding any discussion upon the whole clause, or upon the other counties which are mentioned in the clause. I ask the Prime Minister if he proposes to put a muzzle on this House, and carry out such a ruling as we have just heard. I think we are all anxious to get through with this Bill-a rather unsavoury task, I admit.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: A solemn task.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
He will do it later on in conformity with what his party has been advocating in the committee-that the county of Brant should have two members. Therefore there is no difference of opinion on that point. There are other items on which there is a difference of opinion, and a discussion on these items will be to some purpose. When we come to the district of Victoria and Haliburton, there may be a discussion, because there is a difference of opinion as to whether that district should have one or two members. But in the name of common sense, I appeal to the members of the committee on both sides, why should we waste time discussing
Mr. DEPUTY' SPEAKER.

an item on which both sides are agreed V Let us wait until we come to some point of disagreement, and then we will have a discussion. If my hon. friend from West Toronto (Mr. Clarke) is prepared to contend that the county of Brant should not have two members, we will discuss that point with him; but if he agrees with his party that it should have two members, I think we should allow that item to pass.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I desire to treat the right hon. gentleman with the greatest possible respect, and I want to keep within the rules. I said that I would not agree that the county of Brant and the city of Brantford should have two members at present; and the reason I made that statement is that I want to ask on what principle this representation is to be given in the province of Ontario ? The right hon. gentleman stated yesterday that it was impossible to give urban or thickly settled constituencies the same representation as sparsely settled outlying districts. The district of Victoria and Haliburton has a large area and is sparsely settled; and I ask the right hon. gentleman on what principle does he propose to give a small, compact, well settled urban constituency two representatives, while a large, sparsely settled district, like Victoria and Haliburton, is only to get one ? Iam surely within my right in asking for information in regard to that point, before this clause in reference to Brant and Brantford is adopted.
I am surely entitled to ascertain why sparsely settled districts are to be deprived of the rieht which the right hon. gentleman declared yesterday they should have, if the principle he enunciated is carried out. I need not confine my remarks to Victoria county and Haliburton. What about the county of Hastings with dozens of townships sparsely settled extending away up miles from the front? What principle is to be applied to the representation of that county ? It has a population of 59,291 and is to have two members, while the closely settled urban constituencies of Brant and Brantford, with a population of 38,140, are to have two members. The unit of representation of Brant and Brantford is 19,070 and they form a compact urban constituency. The unit of representation for (the sparsley settled county of Hastings is 29,645. Are the sparsely settled districts of this province, occupying great areas, to be treated in this way ? If the right hon. gentleman's position is sound, that urban constituencies must not expect to have representation by population, I appeal to his sense of justice and fairness that constituen-ciples like Victoria and Haliburton and Hastings shall not be discriminated against. The only opportunity I can have of drawing the right hon. gentleman's attention to this is by discussing the schedule we have before us, because after that is passed the oppor- ,
tunity will be denied me of making comparisons between the representations which are agreed to and those proposed to be given such large districts as Hastings, Victoria and Haliburton.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: My reply to the hon. gentleman is simply this, that both sides in the committee agreed unanimously that the county of Brantford should have two members.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Is that a sufficient reason.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
I think it is. When the committee is unanimous, I shall not go beyond its decisions, and I take it that the point on which it was unanimous is well settled. My hon. friend asks why Haliburton and Hastings have not been treated in the same way. The answer is this, that, so far as Brantford is concerned, there was unanimity, but in the ease of Haliburton and Hastings there was not. My hon. friend's point would be well taken with regard to these two, but not with regard to Brantford, unless he will take the responsibility of refusing to accept the work of the committee where it was unanimous.
ilr. CLARKE. I was appealing to the right hon. gentleman as an umpire to whom we could appeal with a great deal of confidence. He laid down the principle that sparsely settled districts are entitled to greater representation, so far as numbers are concerned, than closely settled urban constituencies, yet we find this principle set aside in the cases I have mentioned.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: No doubt the hon. gentleman's question as to what rules governed the committee is quite fair. Certain well defined rules did govern the committee almost to the letter. There might be something in what the hon. gentleman says about giving a larger representation to the sparsely settled districts, but he must remember that we are limited to 86 representatives for Ontario, and that the House, under the direction of the gov-ment, laid down the principle of county boundaries. Then the committee decided almost unanimously that the unit of population was to be a governing principle. But, according to the hon. gentleman's theory, we could place the great majority of the 86 members in the district of Nipissing. I quite acknowledge that, under some conditions, the unit of representation should be considered and new representation granted to sparsely settled districts. That has been recognized.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Take the county of Bruce.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
Bruce comes strictly under the rule with regard to population, and although this may sometimes appear unjust, when a small county like Prince Edward, with a popula-

tion of 17,800 is in question, there lias to lie some rule governing. Another county may have one member and be within two or three of the unit.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Take the county of Bruce. In the northern part it is very sparsely settled. The unit of representation for Brant and Brantford is 19,007. The county of Bruce has a population of 59,020, so if that large and sparsely settled district is given three members instead of two, the unit of representation for these three would be larger than in the closely compact county of Brant.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: The committee did consider all these points, and in its best judgment unanimously agreed to give two members to the county of Bruce. If the hon. gentleman will look into the matter seriously, he will find great difficulty in suggesting any other rule to govern.	_

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Will the hon. gentleman say that when the rule was laid down a single deviation from it was asked by the Conservative members of the committee. Whenever the rule was violated, it was violated by lion, gentlemen opposite.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: What rule ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I understood the hon. gentleman to say that there was a rule laid down to govern the committee, namely, to take the unit of population at something in excess of 36,000.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: 24,381 was the unit we adopted.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I mean for two members. The unit for a county of two members, I think, was 36,900, or something like that.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: It was 36,572.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: We might as well settle the principle that shall govern the committee. That, it seems to me, is a fair matter for discussion. I said, a moment ago, that the members of the committee representing this side of the House never asked, in a single instance, the slightest deviation from that rule. But that rule has been deviated from in many instances, and in every instance at the suggestion of lion, gentlemen opposite.	.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Will the hon. gentleman (Mr. Clancy) be kind enough, as we are discussing this matter seriously, to point out a single instance in which this rule was departed from ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
Well, take the county of Northumberland with 34,791, which was given two members, although the county of Carleton with 36,000 is given only one. If I were to wait for the hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Sutherland) to rise, he would tell me that the committee unanimously assented to Hon. Mr. SUTHERLAND.
some change in the county of Carleton. I might as well make the matter clear to the committee and save the hon. gentleman the trouble of an explanation, by stating that the Conservative members of the committee were told that if they insisted on following the rule, either one child or the other had to be thrown to the wolves, either Carleton or Leeds.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: My hon. friend (Mr. Clancy) knows that that is not fair or correct.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: That is what we were told after hon. gentlemen had seen the result of the rule to be followed.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: It is not a correct statement of what went on before the committee.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: It was by bringing the splendid legal ability of the Minister of Justice (Hon. Mr. Fitzpatrick) to bear that they made the discovery that opened the way to the object they sought. It was understood that unions of counties would not be considered as territorial divisions but that they would be considered as counties. But hon. gentlemen opposite found that they could not in that way gain the advantage they sought, so they applied to the Minister of Justice. That hon. gentleman declared that a union of counties was a county, and so they decided that they would follow that rule. The Conservatives were told : You had better look out ; if you insist on two members for the county of Carleton we will unite all these counties and that would be worse for you. So, in the absence of any rule that could be reasonably followed, the committee, the Conservative members of the committee were forced to make a choice of evils.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: As a lialf-loaf.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
Yes-not justice, but the best that could be had. Peterborough is not entitled to two members, nor is Northumberland. So, when the Prime Minister says that all have agreed that Brant should have two members, he sajfs what is. quite true, but surely he will not insist that this clause should be considered by itself, leaving out of account other counties that are even more entitled to two members than is the county of Brant. If you have representation according to population, the right hon. gentleman will see that, notwithstanding that the committee agreed to this, it is not reasonable that (Brant should have two members while other larger counties should have only one.
The MINISTER OF PuBLIC WORKS. If the hon. gentleman (Mr. Clancy) does not agree with the rule adopted by the committee, what rule would he suggest for dealing with these counties ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
I will tell the hon. gentleman the rule I would suggest; and I am

sure that the hon. members on this side would all agree to. Bet us lay down a rule of population on the basis of which it is to be decided whether a county shall have one or two members, and let us follow that rule, no matter where it strikes. We are prepared to abide by such a rule, no matter how it affects us.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: In the amendments handed in by the opposition, Brantford, with a population of only 10,519, is given one member. This is just over the unit. Yet, London, with 37,900, considerably over double that unit, is given only one member.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: The hon. gentleman cannot hold us responsible for that. The city of London, according to the unit of population, would be entitled to two members ; and we are prepared to give London two members. Let us follow the rule, and we shall not ask that it be deviated from by a hair's breadth. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Hyman) refused to have two members for London, because it suited his purpose better to violate the rule. The right hon. gentleman (Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier) seems very much amused. I do not know whether it is because of the inconsistency of his own friends or of the advantages he sees that he will gain under this Bill.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Both.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Very likely. Now, Middlesex county is given three members. It has a population of 54,526. On the other hand, take the following counties that, are given only two members :	Wellington, population 55,646 ; Lambton, 56,642 ; Kent, 57,422 ; Essex, 58,516 ; Bruce, 59,020, and Hastings, 59,291.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: May I ask the hon. gentleman (Mr. Clancy) if he has deducted the urban population in making up these figures, as he deducted the urban population of London in making up the figures for the county of Middlesex ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: As the hon. gentleman knows perfectly well the cities, including London, Hamilton, Toronto, Kingston and Ottawa are made exceptions and are dealt with separately.

speechtext: Made exception by whom '!

speechtext: By both parties. Why, the hon. gentleman (Mr. Hyman) laid it down in his own schedule, submitted to the Conservative members of the committee.

speechtext: And the right hon. Prime Minister, in introducing the Bill did the same.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Yrou cannot include the city of London in the county of Middlesex any more than you include the city of Toronto in the county of York. And I must say. it comes with rather bad grace from the hon. gentleman (Mr. Hyman), representing the city of London in this House, in this peevish, childish way, to refuse to give his own city two members, though it is entitled to that number under the rule of population which the hon. gentleman himself favours, and to insist on the county getting three members when it is only entitled to two.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I am forced to call attention again to the fact that this discussion, in my opinion is wholly irrelevant to the question before the committee. maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I think the chairman is quite right in saying that when we are discussing a section we should confine ourselves to it. speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Before the hon. gentleman proceeds, I want to say that the principle of the division made by the committee has been under discussion for two or three days, and yesterday a motion was made for the House to resolve itself into Committee of the Whole. maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
The Prime Minister will remember that just as soon ns this was read, I drew his attention to the fact that some of us might desire to make reference to other clauses having relation to the one under discussion. The PRIME MINISTER, That is not oil the point of order.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I do not think any of these particular clauses should be discussed apart from the whole section. maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I would like to understand the effect of this ruling. After we have passed the clause for Brant and come to another county, cannot Brant be referred to by comparison ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: It can be referred to, but not discussed.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I cannot see how we can proceed in that way.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: For instance, you cannot discuss Middlesex without discussing Elgin, because you are taking away from Middlesex and putting into Elgin.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: My point is that we cannot discuss one county without comparison with another. You can only tell the size of a mountain by comparing it with another.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I do not understand, Mr. Chairman, that by your ruling we could not refer to another county by way of comparison, but that we cannot discuss afi item that has been passed. Certainly we have no intention to restrict the discussion. But I thought that these clauses might be passed concerning which wo are agreed; for instance, there need be no dismission on Carleton, Dundas, Dufferin or Durham, also Brant; but when we come to the county of Victoria, then there may be discussion, because there is a difference of opinion. I do not see why hon. gentlemen on the other side cannot agree to pass those which will occasion no discussion, and where there is no intention of disturbing the findings of the committee.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
I think the point raised as to narrowing the discussion, and not being able to make comparisons, is an important one. My hon. friend from West Toronto (Mr. Clarke), discussing the city of Brant, took occasion to make a comparison as to population. I think that the whole of this clause 2 is now under discussion. The Chairman read the beginning of that clause Mr. HUGHES (Victoria).
very rapidly, and passed on to the next one. I think a certain latitude should-be allowed us, as long as there is no evident intention of prolonging the discussion uselessly. As to what has been said in relation to the county of Brant and its limits, that must necessarily come up under clause 27.
