maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: When this matter was before the committee certain propositions were submitted by the Conservative members for the guidance of the committee in the course of the discussion. .The first proposition adopted was the principle laid down by the Prime Minister, that is to say, that municipal county boundaries should be observed.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: What page ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I am not reading from any page. We had 92 constituencies in Ontario, and it was necessary to reduce those down to 86. In making that reduction it was necessary for us to apply certain principles. Here are the principles that were laid down for our guidance by the Conservative members of the committee :	Each county or combined county having a population of not less than 36.572. that is to say. 50 per cent niore than the unit, shall be entitled to two members, and each county or combined county having a population of not less than 60,953, that is to say, not less than two and a half per cent of the unit, shall be entitled to three members. That is what the Conservative members of the committee asked us to do.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Has the hon. gentleman followed it ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
I was about to say to the committee when this unnecessary interruption was made, and I would not qualify it otherwise, that we applied that principle to Brant. We had to give two members to Brant because the population of Brant entitles it to two members it having more than 36,572. W'e attempted to dispose of Brant first. Then, after disposing of Brant, we found that there were other counties that had to be provided for when the counties that are entitled to two members are provided for. -it is found that if any seats remain to be allotted, such seats shall be allotted^ to the counties cr combined counties approaching most closely to the conditions which, under the above rule, would entitle them to additional representation.
So, the first thing to do is to dispose of those counties that are entitled to one or more- members and if after you have done that there are other districts not provided for they must be joined on to existing con-

stituencies. That is the principle upon which we acted.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: It is true that this rule was proposed and I think it would have been a wise rule for our guidance but it was not accepted. The hon. Minister of Justice will remember that in regard to the first three rules there was a disposition to accept but. that they were not formerly accepted. These were set aside. I say that for my part I am quite prepared to adhere to these rules. It seems to me that these rules were wise and it seems to me that the rule which the hon. Minister of Justice has referred is being applied to the consideration of Brant but this does not prevent my hon. friend from West Toronto (Mr. Clarke) under the rules of order from asking to compare the population of this constituency with that of others. That is the point of order.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: May I ask the hon. gentleman the page of those notes he was reading from ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I do not know that my hon. friend has this. This is a copy of the proposals in respect to the redistribution in Ontario submitted by the Conservative members of the committee.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: They are in the proceedings.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: They will come in very handy for reference. But, I understand the hon. Minister of Justice to say that the considerations which bound the committee were first, an adherence to municipal and county boundaries, and second, the question of population.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
Yes, an adherence to municipal and county boundaries except in respect to those counties where by mutual consent we departed from that principle. Then, in respect to population. the question was settled on the lines that I have laid down. It does seem curious that I cannot make myself clear. If I used my own language it might not be clear but I am using the language of the hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden, Halifax) when he says that the rule to be adopted is that each county having a population of not less than 3G,572 is to be entitled to two members. That is what he says and that is the rule we have applied to Brant. Therefore that disposes of the matter. The hon. member for Bothwell (Mr. Clancy) spoke a moment ago of some opinion I gave in connection with this matter. I just simply took the well considered, carefully drafted and deliberately submitted resolution and I applied the law to it. Hon. gentlemen have said, for instance, that:
If after applying these principles it is found that any seats remain to be allotted, sucdi seats shall be allotted to the counties or combined counties approaching most closely to the 344
conditions 'which, under the above rule, would entitle them to additional representation.
_ They had not carefully read the Revised Statutes or they would have known that section 3 of the Revised Statutes provides that a united county is a county for municipal purposes and it is because they fell into that error that they are dissatisfied. It is not my fault but the fault of the law.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: The hon. gentleman need not fancy that he stands alone in having an opinion which is supported by law. There is no one who will doubt the hon. gentleman's ability as a lawyer, but, lawyers differ and quite as good lawyers as the hon. gentleman do not hold this opinion. The hon. gentleman has given some light to the country. After having honourably sat down with the committee, after having invited them to his table as his guests he found or imagined he found they had made some mistake and he was honourable enough to take advantage of it. But, I want to go back to this other question, and to one part of it in regard to which the hon. gentleman has given an explanation. If the rule had been followed there would have been no need of this discussion at all, because Victoria.and Haliburton would have been entitled to two members instead of Brant when the choice fell between them. If we were to pass Brant now when these combined counties are entitled to consideration we might find that they were excluded. I want to ask the right lion, leader of the government if he proposes to adhere to the rule as laid down and accepted by the Minister of Justice because he was the party who accepted it and to follow the rule without any exception.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: My hon. friend (Mr. Clancy) is rather exacting when he says that we shall follow the rule without any exception. I do not know of any rule in grammar or anywhere else which has not its exceptions. But my hon. friend is too exacting altogether. I would have hoped that he would have had some confidence in his leader, because his leaders have agreed to this, and I would have hoped that lie would have abided by their decision. I do not know whether or not his leaders have been bribed by my colleague, because, if so, perhaps they are not entitled to the same consideration. I have no such conflict with his leaders as he has, because, when the leaders have determined upon giving two members to Brant, I am quite willing to do so. When we come to item 20 ' the county of Victoria, with the provisional- county of Haliburton,' if there is a difference of opinion between his leaders and my colleagues on that committee, affording a reasonable ground for discussion I am quite willing that we should discuss the whole subject, although there is really no difference of opinion between the two sides of the House.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: There is a striking difference of opinion. Victoria and Haliburton are better entitled to two members than Brant, and therefore, if we pass Brant as it is in the Bill, it will he useless to discuss the question of Victoria and Haliburton. The only way to remedy that is to hold Brant, and if it is found that the population of Victoria and Haliburton are better entitled to additional representation we can give Victoria and Haliburton an additional member and give Brant one member. But. to pass Brant is perfectly idle with the view to reaching the other because in the meantime the arrangement in regard to Brant would have been assented to. It was assented to because it was believed that Victoria and Haliburton would have two.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Not at all. Victoria and Haliburton do not exist as a municipality.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: But they are combined counties.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: But we deal only with Victoria.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: The hon. gentleman in his Bill states that they are combined counties.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: They are not combined counties within the meaning of the statute.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I would like then, to ask the hon. the Minister of Justice why he is dealing with them V

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Because you have the provisional district of Haliburton that has to be disposed of and for the purpose of disposing of it you join it to Victoria.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: And give it no representation.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Yes, it gets all the representation it is entitled to. If my hon. friends will look across the House they will see the representation.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: As we have had much discussion about the county of Victoria and Haliburton perhaps it would facilitate the proceedings if we had a little light on the subject. I am going to give a comparison and to reason from the case of Brant and to ask the Prime Minister why he proposes to give Brant an extra member. I will also point out that he should give an extra member to Bruce instead of to Brant.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: We will come to Bruce and Victoria and Haliburton later on.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I am discussing Brant.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
lit is mot pleasant for me to sit in my seat when I know that the whole committee is out of Sir WILFRID LAIJRIER.
order. My ruling is that the discussion will have to be confined to the item before the committe. To refer for purposes of illustration to a county or division which we have already7 passed is, however, quite within the liberty of any hon. member.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: That is exactly what I am doing.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: But it is not proper to discuss the propriety of a division upon which we have already passed although we can refer to it as an illustration.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I am actiug in accordance with the ruling of the chairman and I am right in pointing out my reasons why I think the Prime Minister should not allow the Bill to pass in its present _ form. maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Before leaving Brant might I ask if, when we resume the discussion of Brantford, we can get information as to why this county is to be given representation on a unit of 19,070, which is the population of the county of Brant and the city of Brantford ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Oh, no.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: And why the outlying districts constituting Bruce will be given representation only on a unit of 29,510 and why the county of Hastings, another county of which the northern part is sparsely settled, is given representation on the basis of a unit of 29,645, while a well settled metropolitan county such as Middlesex is given representation on the basis of 18,242 and Brant, as I have stated, on the basis of 19,070 7

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I think I will be able to satisfy my hon. friend on that point.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: If it is desired to pass over Brant, I have no objection, but I would say that Brant is only being made an excuse. If the mind of the committee was that Victoria and Haliburton should have two members instead of one and that therefore some other county lias to _ give up one member, there are two or three counties with a less population than Brant. There are Peterborough. Lanark and Leeds, so that there is no reason for holding Brant at all.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: It is information of that kind we want.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: The right lion, gentleman has said that the committee were unanimous that Brant should have two members, that is not disputed on this side.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: No, it is not.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: But surely the hon. gentleman does not wish us to believe that they were unanimous also as to how the county of Brant should be divided.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: No.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Then I understand they were not unanimous so far as the county ot Brant is concerned.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
I desire to make a few observations on the remarks of the Minister of Justice in reference to the principles that guided the committee in their deliberations. In speaking of county boundaries he said that only municipal county boundaries were to be observed. We perfectly agreed to that, and when the committee was appointed we accepted it under the dictum of the right lion, gentleman who leads the government, who said that that was one of the principles to be observed. I was particular at the first meeting to ascertain what was meant by a municipal county boundary. The Minister of Justice stated that municipal county boundaries meant the divisions established under the clause of the Revised Statutes of Ontario. I drew7 the attention of the Minister of Justice to the fact that under that , Act there were united counties; there were the counties of Leeds and Grenville, Lennox and Addington and others. I asked the Minister of Justice if he was going to exercise the power of delimitation within the united counties in the same way as if they were ordinary counties. He said :	No, that the comities
were to be the original counties as united and that we were not to exercise that power within them. We had an understanding then among the members of the committee, and my hon. friend the leader of the opposition fell into no trap at all; he was putting the same interpretation on the word ' county ' as the Minister of Justice put on it.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
My hon. friend surely does not intend to be inaccurate but he certainly has not read the Revised Statutes of Ontario. For municipal purposes the united counties are municipal counties; the united county is a municipal entity and if you speak of the municipal county of Stormont, Dundas and Glengarry you refer to their boundaries, but within the limits of the municipal county there are the subdivisions of the county which have no municipal existence but which have a geographical existence. Take for instance the united county of Stormont, Dundas and Glengarry; that is one municipal entity, but you have again the geographical county of 344J
Stormont which has a separate existence from Glengarry and Dundas and we have never departed from that principle. I defy hon. gentlemen opposite to point out a single case in which we have departed.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: The hon. minister must think me very dense if he thinks I cannot understand a single proposition.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Any one of the three is a geographical entity but the anited county of Stormont, Dundas and Glengarry includes the three of them.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: That is the union of three counties. My question to the hon. gentleman was this : w'hether we would be at liberty to take a portion of one of these counties and add it to another ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: In not a single case have we done that.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I am not saying that the committee did. But the hon. gentleman said that my leader fell into a trap, when he interpreted a county as being distinct from united counties. I understood at that time that the three entities constituted the whole county, and that a portion of one of them was not to be added to another.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: That has been followed.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: That has been followed, but we came to that understanding afterwards. The Minister of Justice took a different view in the committee until the hon. leader of the opposition moved the amendment. He took the position that the resolution proposed by Mr. Borden gave the power of delimitation anywhere within the united counties ; and in order to get an agreement from the whole committee that nothing of that kind should be done, I proposed that Carleton should have only one member, and Leeds one member, with the understanding that there should be no delimitation within the united counties.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: We will suspend this clause.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Can you suspend a clause without the consent of the whole committee ? In my humble opinion, that clause has not been suspended, because the question has never been submitted to the committee. You are willing to suspend it, but perhaps I am not willing, and I will give my reason why I think it should not be suspended.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: There are a lot of counties on which I think there is no difference of opinion, and I do not see why we should not pass them.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
I want to know if that question in reference to Brantford has been suspended. I contend that it has not, and I want to speak to the question. It appears

to me that the humblest member of this committee is entitled to some information when he wants it. It is all well enough for you, Mr. Chairman, to dictate to the committee, and to say that things are carried when they are not carried.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Order.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I am not saying anything offensive to the chairman, or any one else in this House. I think I have some rights here, and I am going to exercise them. The information I want is this : We have a ruling of the Chair that we must confine our discussion to the question whether the county of Brant is entitled to two members. I understood from the Premier that the rule was not going to be applied, as we could not discuss whether representation was going to be properly given if we confined our discussion to one county. And I want to say that hon. gentlemen opposite will not promote the passing of this Bill in an agreeable manner by referring to another gerrymander. That has been a heart-burning question in this House in the past. If that was a mistake. I expected that when this R dis.rih. tio.i Bill was referred to a committee. it was going to be dealt with fairly to both parties. It is just as well to let bygones be bygones, and not refer to past contentions ; because we could easily refer to the iniquities perpetrated by the party of hon. gentlemen opposite in the local house. So it is just as well to leave these matters alone. For my part, I feel very keenly in reference to this measure. There are just as gross iniquities perpetrated under this fair-looking scheme as there were under the old one. I may be wrong, but the only way to convince a man like myself is by a judicial reference of the matter, instead of bringing up things that we did. The Minister of Justice and the Premier said that when the committee assented to a thing, we should not take any exception to it.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: No, I did not argue that.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I do not want the Minister of Justice to cast any reflections on any member of this House because he has not studied the Act. I have heard the Minister of Justice ask members of this House what a certain law meant when I thought he ought to have known. We find that the Minister of Justice sometimes does not understand the law as well as he might.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I admit that.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I am glad that we have arrived at a satisfactory conclusion in regard to that. There are some points of law which I find lawyers do not know until the courts settle them. I do not want the members of the legal profession to decide that they know it all until the courts decide. The Minister of Justice said that the county of Brant was divided on a certain principle;

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: but when you try to carry out that principle everywhere, you find that you cannot do it, because you would have to provide for too many members. The committee laid down the principle that a certain population should elect a member, and that where the population was more than that, there should be two members ; but, in working out that principle, they found that they could not apply it all round. I want to ask the Minister of Justice did the majority of that committee consent to that principle being adopted ? As I understand, they admitted it where it suited them from a political point of view : but where it did not they would not admit it. They admitted it in Brant, because that county would probably return two reformers ; but they would not admit it in Hastings, because that county would probably return three Tories. If I am wrong in saying this, I wish to be put right. When you come to examine the Bill all along the line, you will find that the unit of population was all right where it would probably return Liberals, but it was all wrong where it was going probably to return Tories. What did the hon. gentleman then treat as municipal and county boundaries ? Glengarry-there was no talk of uniting Glengarry with any other county then; Prescott, Stormont, Russell, Dundas, Carleton, Grenville, Frontenac, Kingston, Lennox, Addington, Prince Edward, Dur-lmm, Peel, Halton, Dufferin, Wentworth, Norfolk, Welland, Nipissing, Haliburton, Muskoka, Parry Sound and Thunder Bay. Now, I wish to point out to the Prime Minister the reason I asked for the ease of Carleton to stand. It. is because, in its consideration, they were unwillingly forced to consent to that as a
choice between two evils. speechtext: I desire to say a few words as regards the formation of the north riding of Grey. Mr. Snyder, Liberal, was elected for North Grey. He also carried that constituency in 1S72. and in 1874. In 1878, Mr. Lane, a Conservative, carried it. In 1882 it returned a Liberal. In 1887 Mr. Masson, Conservative, was elected. In 1891 he was returned again. In 1896 it elected Mr. Clarke, a Liberal. In 1896 Mr. Paterson, Liberal, was elected. In 1900, the late Dr. Horsey was returned, and in 1903 your humble servant. One might have expected that the Minister of Customs would have endeavoured to keep this old constituency within the bounds in which it has stood since confederation. One would have thought that he would have looked back with considerable gratitude to that constituency for having afforded him an asylum when he was driven out of Brant, and that out of gratitude he would not have allowed its boundaries to be interfered with. I may explain here that the city of Chatham is upon both sides of the river, and can ns readily be put in one riding as in the other. It is upon the four corners of four townships. Two of them, namely, Dover and Chatham, are on the north side, and Harwich and Raleigh are divided on the north side of the river. By taking the proposition of the hon. gentleman, East Kent would then be constituted of the township of Chatham, Walllaceburg. Camden. Dresden, Thamesville Zone, Orford, Howard and Rjdgetown. That is the proposal made by the hon. gentleman in plan No. 1. The right hon. gentleman

I would like to say a word about this eoujty. I have had the honour of representing Kent for a good many years in this House, and I must say that it requires a good deal of assurance on the part of the hon. member for Bothwell (Mr. Clancy) to get up and talk the way he does about this redistribution. Of all the mean things that were done in 1882, the way in which Bothwell was cut and carved to suit the Conservative party was the meanest of all. There was no possible excuse for it except to defeat the Hon. David Mills. Kent is composed of Kent and Bothwell. It was divided at confederation into two equal parts without dividing the townships as near as could be. When divided in that way it returned a Conservative, and it also returned the Hon. David Mills, but in order to defeat Mr. Mills, one of the meanest, one of the most cold-blooded things that was ever perpetrated by any parliament in Canada was done in 1882, when the townships of Howard, Oxford and the town of Ridgetown were taken away from Bothwell, to which they belonged municipally and in every other way, and put into West Elgin, where they did not belong at all, and where the people had nothing to do with each other, simply because these townships gave a Liberal majority, and it was hoped in this way to defeat the Hon. David Mills. In order to make up the population what did they do ? They took the township of Chatham from West Kent and put it into Bothwell in order to make up the population of Bothwell, because Chatham gave a Conservative majority. They did not equalize the population, they did not make a better shaped county than before, they did not suit the convenience of the people at all, in fact they disarranged tlie whole machinery of the county in order to defeat the Hon. David Mills. They did that deliber-Mr. CLANCY.
ately and in cold blood, and the hon. member for Bothwell sat in this House all these long years and never raised his voice against it. Did they equalize the population ? No, Sir, the difference in the population was greater after the redistribution that it was before, and in order to defeat a prominent member of the Liberal party they took these two townships and put them into West Elgin, and then took Chatham township, which did not belong there at all, and put it into Bothwell again. By this Bill we are simply restoring the two townships where they originally belonged. We take the whole county of Kent and we divide it into East and' West Kent, as it should be. The hon. member for Bothwell (Mr. Clancy) proposes to take the town of Chatham away from West Kent on the other side of the River Thames, and put it in the north riding and form a new county there. He takes Howard, Orford and Ridgetown, which were never in West Kent at at all, but always in Bothwell, and wants to put them into West Kent and to make a new county formed of townships that were never before associated in any way in order to make a safe seat for himself. He would have no pangs of conscience over the rascally, the outrageous, the scandalous way in which that county was treated by his friends twenty years ago.

In the outset he stated one thing that was utterly destitute of fact, that Bothwell and a portion of Kent were formerly equally and fairly divided. I am not going to say whether the redistribution of 1882 was right < r wrong and I am not going to say that the right hon. the Prime Minister was not honest and moved by proper motives, when he stated that although there were great temptations-to use his own words-to retort and to punish those who punished the Liberal party, he was not disposed to take that course. deuce with regard to Bothwell is that the I Hon. David Mills was elected year after year up to 1896, when he was defeated. The River Thames is a boundary line between the two townships, one on the north and the other on the south. Chatham is on both sides of the river and no one would undertake to say that the riding would be of a less symmetrical shape if the river was taken as a dividing line.

If population is to be considered no one would argue that you should make a difference of nearly 7,000 in the population. Of course we know what the object of this is, it is that no Conservative would have a reasonable chance of being elected if the Liberal vote is polled as it has been in the past. maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
I have an amendment to move. Believing, as I do, that the province of Prince Edward Island is entitled to six members, and that we are being deprived by the government of Canada of our rights in that regard, I move :
(a.) The county of King's shall form an electoral district, to be called the electoral district of King's, and shall return two members.
Ob.) The county of Prince shall form an electoral district, to be called the electoral district of Prince, and shall return two members.
(c.) The county of Queen's shall form an electoral district, to be called the district of Queen's, and shall return two members.
I move this amendment to place before this parliament the rights of Prince Edward Island in this regard. I trust the amendment will be accepted by the government and will be allowed to pass.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: The object of my hon. friend (Mr. Hackett) is to provide that Prince Edward Island shall have six members, instead of four, and he asks the government to approve of his motion. I have to say that the government have no option in this matter. This point was referred to the Supreme Court, and that court has decided that Prince Edward Island is entitled to only four members, New Brunswick to thirteen, Nova Scotia to eighteen, and so on. We cannot disregard that.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
I regret to hear this statement. For, when Prince Edward Island entered the union it was perfectly understood by the people of that province that

the representation in this House should never go below six. As to the provisions ot the British North America Act in this connection, I contend that they apply only in the case of an increase, that Prince Edward Island has been entitled to six members from the time of confederation, and that to cut down that representation is to invade the rights of the province. The people there believe that, in surrendering their rights as an independent colony of the empire and joining the Canadian Federation they would receive just and generous treatment from the Dominion. Lord Grenville, as I quoted last night in his message to the government of Canada in 1870, laid down the principle that you should deal generously and justly with the people of Prince Edward Island. It would be quite erroneous to think that the people of Prince Edward Island is becoming a part of confederation with a representation of six members in this House did so with the idea that they might be deprived of any of that representation. I trust the right hon. gentleman the right hon. Prime Minister will change his mind and allow the province to have its true representation.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: My hon. friend (Mr. Hackett) will understand that this is a matter over which neither the government nor the parliament would have any control. If it were in the power of parliament to grant two additional members to Prince Edward Island, as the hon. gentleman proposes, I have no doubt parliament would be willing to do so. But parliament is bound by law, and there is the decision of the Supreme Court, which says that under the returns of the last census Prince Edward Island is entitled to only four members. I am informed that the government of Prince Edward Island are taking steps to have this decision of the Supreme Court carried to the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council. So, we are not doing injustice to Prince Edward Island, but simply treating it according to the decision of the Supreme Court, to which court the matter was referred.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I have here the opinion of the Minister of Justice (Hon. Mr. Fitzpatrick) who stands at the head of the law in this country. He says that parliament has the right in connection with the imperial parliament to pass a resolution of this kind without any alteration in the legislation.

friends-I do not recollect 'whether he was a member here in 1882-changed his constituency from what it was. It has been readjusted from time to time. But there were special reasons in regard to Carleton and Russell, why they should remain as they are.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I did not say that changes should not be made. I followed up the statement made by the hon. member for London (Mr. Hyman), who seemed to be influenced by the consideration that where a constituency had remained in one condition for a long time no change should be made. The hon. gentleman has no right to say I am drawing upon my imagination. I did not wish to repeat a statement I made here to-night, but the hon. gentleman forces me to do so. I wish to say, in the presence of the hon. member for South Lanark (Hon. Mr. Haggart) and the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk), on this side, and the hon. Minister of Public Works (Hon. Mr. Sutherland) and the hon. member for London (Mr. Hyman), on the other side, that the proposition came from and was pressed by some hon. gentleman from that side, and that hon. gentlemen on this side would have preferred to stand by the rule. Is a member to be told that he is drawing on his imagination because of statements of that kind ? My right hon. friend (Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier) seems very much amused.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: If the hon. gentleman will not accept my word, I would refer him to the record of the committee, which is supposed to be correct. I stated distinctly at the time to the leader of the opposition that we were willing to either follow the rule or to make a variation.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I would like to ask if it was left optional with the members on the committee who are on this side to adopt the rule or to accept the hon. gentleman's proposition ? If he states that it was optional, I am bound to say I have been unjust to him.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Apologize.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: The right hon. gentleman knows that, if I am in the wrong, I am ready to apologize, far more ready than his friends would be in such a case. If the hon. Minister of Public Works will say that this was optional, I am willing to acknowledge that I have done him an injustice. But I venture to say in advance that he will not make that statement. So, it is not fair to say that I have been drawing on my imagination.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
Has not the hon. gentleman heard the hon. member for South Lanark say that this was a matter of compromise, and that he had yielded on the point of having two members for Carleton,
and accepted the proposition that there should be only one, because there were to he two for Leeds and Grenville, and he also pulled the wool over the eyes of the hon. member for East Peterborough (Mr. Lang). And yet, my hon. friend (Mr. Clancy) is not satisfied.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
Discussing the point raised by the hon. member for Bothwell (Mr. Clancy), I find I am quoted in the proceedings of the committee, at page 202. Discussing this question of county boundaries, we had before us the two propositions. The chairman is on record as saying :
I am perfectly willing to proceed under this clause under the principle laid down that municipal county boundaries shall be observed.
That was clear.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Will the hon. gentleman tell me if municipal county boundaries as first understood by the committee was in accordance with the interpretation of the Minister of Justice ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: The hon. Minister of Justice can speak for himself. In my opinion the hon. gentleman (Mr. Clancy) has no right to say that the Minister of Justice ever changed his mind with regard to the law on this subject. For my part, having some municipal and provincial experience, I knew before the Act was turned up what was meant by a municipal county in the province of Ontario. When the leader of the opposition submitted his proposal, I accepted it knowing that probably we would have to change the schedule that we had submitted in an informal way, and for the purpose of facilitating business. And surely the hon. gentleman will do us the justice to remember that, even after having accepted the rule, we were willing to meet the members of the opposition, by making certain changes, or we were willing to stand by the schedule we had first made as to the single counties. There is no evidence of unfairness there. Had we accepted the proposition in its entirety and desired to take advantage of it- that is the proposition submitted by the leader of the opposition himself-we might have divided these counties, perhaps, to our own political advantage. We neither attempted nor desired to do anything of that kind. We at once decided that we would deal with these counties as decided in the first place, keeping as close as possible to the principle of county boundaries.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
It seems to me that our friends from Ontario labour under a considerable disadvantage at this particular stage of the discussion. I am not reproaching any particular person for the failure to print the proceedings of the committee. As a matter of fact, I remember that when we parted at our last meeting, it was agreed that typewritten copies should be made for

the use of members of the committee. I never got my own, probably because I did not call for it. But it is a matter of regret that, as we are discussing this question now, the argument comes up over and over again, that such and such a matter was agreed to by the committee, and our friends who are deeply interested in this subject are not able immediately to refer to the part of the discussion in the committee where these agreements or supposed agreements are recorded.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: If the hon. gentleman will allow me, though we have not the arguments or reasons, we have the results in every case.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: We have the amendments. As to that, I may say that I never saw these printed amendments until yesterday, when I saw them in the hands of my hon. friend from East Grey (Mr. Sproule). I went to the distribution office to get a copy, and was handed a copy by the clerk there, who told me that I could not be allowed more than one copy. I never received a copy through the mail, and some of my hon. friends tell me that they are in the same position. But there is a discussion which has been recorded

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: The hon. Minister of Justice tells me that he inquired of the clerk of distribution, and was informed that these documents were distributed in the ordinary way.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
I do not deny that. I only say that I did not receive a copy. As this discussion is carried on, when a constituency is taken up for discussion my hon. friends on this side must refer to the typewritten copy of what was said, using the two copies which my hon. friend* from South Lanark (Hon. Mr. Haggart) and myself have at our disposal. They must look through about 350 pages of typewritten matter, which is not indexed. If my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works were asked to state the facts with regard to Lanark, Middlesex or Victoria, he could not do it readily. I have been trying to make an index with regard to the counties which are the subject of disagreement. Then when the question of population c mes up. the census must be referred to. The Minister of Justice has sent me a book which has been prepared in most convenient form for reference. Everything is indexed. and you can turn at once to any given constituency. This is necessary, no doubt, for the minister to have. It is a very convenient book for the hon. minister and his friends to have at their disposal. Then, there is the configuration of the counties which is to be found in the electoral maps of the Dominion, and which we had in the committee. But each one of my hon. friends has not got one of these maps. Besides, these maps are not indexed, and it is diffi-Mr. MONK.
cult to find any given county. Under these circumstances, we must proceed very slowly. Moreover, my hon. friends are obliged to have a set of documents in hand which it is difficult to handle while they are making their arguments to the committee. Now, as we have advanced the work considerably, I suggest agaiii that it is advisable, for the expedition of the work when it comes up again, that we stop now.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: My hon. friend will remember that the chairman of the committee had to work out a great deal of this information from the census returns and other books, and he had a number of copies made showing the ridings, when the change was'lnade, the population, and so forth, and each member of the committee was furnished with a copy. Perhaps my hon. friend has lost his.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I think we ought to have a record of the amendments proposed in the committee respecting the schedules of this Bill. Will the hon. gentleman tell us some of the resolutions moved by the majority that were not carried by the committee? What became of those motions ? Are they on record?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: We got power from the House to engage a clerk and stenographer, and they kept track of all these things. It is not very likely that the majority of the committee would propose amendments and vote them down. At the same time, propositions made by the majority of the committee were changed from time to time. After discussion, we came to a conclusion and agreed upon what was best to be done. I do not know if there is any record of that. But many changes were made with regard to these constituencies during the long time the committee were at work.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Then some of the motions were defeated by the committee ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: They were not all defeated. I think the leader of the opposition said he was anxious to discuss some of those matters with his friends, and desired! the privilege of placing that document in the hands of the clerk of the committee before it was printed, in order to put in some amendments that he might desire to make after consultation with his friends.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
This is a very important Bill, and many of its clauses are contentious and likely to take up several days in discussion. I think the right hon. gentleman should put some person in charge of these volumes and have them indexed for the convenience of members. While this committee was in conference, they asked each member of the House to appear before then and state why their particular county ought

to be changed, or why it should remain intact. Now, we have no evidence of that in this document. If we had an index of that evidence it would save a good deal of time in the discussion. For my part. I must say that the gentleman who drew this Bill, if he had desired to make it ns inconvenient as possible for us to discuss it, he could not have done it more effectually. Take the province of Ontario, which involves 54 sections with several paragraphs. Now, would it be any hardship to put under one head all the constituencies commencing with A, under another all those commencing with B, and so forth, then each man could put his finger on it in a moment. Suppose I ask tlie hon. member for Essex (Mr, Cowan), who has the Bill in his hands, to tell me where Essex is.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Clause 27.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Not at all.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: That is what the hon. gentleman has been talking about.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: It just shows he does not know. Then, we come to the chairman, who, I presume, has orders to take advantage of the members of the opposition, and just as soon as a member of the opposition takes his seat for the purpose of looking up a point, the chairman declares the item carried. Now, does the right hon, gentleman expect us to make much progress under those circumstances ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
I would suppose that after the committee had taken power to employ a stenographer and a clerk, a correct record would have been made of all motions moved and carried by the committee. That was the course in 1892 when we had a long committee of inquiry, and a copy of the proceedings was given to every member of the committee and to many members of the House so that we could review the work of the previous day to see what had been done. If it was worth while to employ a stenographer it seems to me that a copy of the report of the proceedings of the committee should have been furnished to the House, because, afterwards, these proceedings must be reviewed by the House. I have heard the argument addressed to hon. gentlemen on this side of the House several times to-night, which seems to be a very improper argument, that this was agreed to unanimously by the committee and that we therefore must not object to it. Are we legislating by committee or by parliament ? Is it .not the usual course that all Bills after going to a committee come back to us and the House then resolves itself into a committee of the whole to consider these Bills clause by clause, and when a clause is under consideration it is the right, no matter whether it is agreed to or not by the committee unanimously or otherwise, of any hon. member to criticise each clause and to move
an amendment >f lie so desires. T'ur; is a right belonging to every member of parliament and he does nothing improper when he exercises that right. We have frequently heard it said across the floor of tins House :	You are discrediting your oiwn
men who were members of the committee by challenging what was done. Not by any means. If parliament were only legislating by committee it might be said that such was the case, but surely, in regard to this measure, we must pursue the same course that we do in regard to every measure that comes before the House and every hon. member is within his right and he is only discharging his duty when he criticises every clause of this Bill no matter whether it was unanimously agreed to or otherwise. But, in addition to that, if we were expected to pay attention to what was done by the committee, as we at least on this side of the House desire to do. we ought to have had the record of its work from day to day before us so that in the meantime, before we came to this discussion, we could have made ourselves familiar with it and reached the conclusion we desired to reach in regard to the outlines of the various constituencies that we have to deal with here. I think this omission to supply us with the record was very improper. We ought to have had it indexed as well so that there would be no trouble in turning up the subject that we desired to turn up at a moment's notice, the inability to do which has been a cause of delay. The great bulk of the members of this House have practically little information in regard to what took place in that committee, and yet, when the concrete Bill that has been brought in is placed before us we are expected to pass it en bloc, because 'hon. gentlemen say it has been agreed to by a committee composed of four members from one side of the House and three from the other side. I think that is unreasonable. It has been proposed that we might very properly adjourn to-night because we have done so much. That suggestion was made because of a desire on this side of the House to have a conference amongst ourselves and reach an understanding as to what features or clauses of the Bill we would address ourselves to, because we have been unable to do that owing to the very meagre information which has been given to us. I may say that I only .got the document which embodies the resolutions of the opposition this afternoon. That was the first I saw of it. If it was distributed in our boxes we knew nothing of it, and as a result we jhave had no time to carefully go over it. The Bill may have been distributed, but it only came into our hands yesterday and consequently we had very little time tb consider it. It does seem to me that we would be facilitating the business quite as much if we had an opportunity of talking that matter over amongst ourselves. We did

so in some measure at noon and also after the House rose at sics o'clock and the result has been that we have made much better progress since. The only desire we have is to get a better knowledge of the provisions of the Bill before we are called upon to discuss it in the House.
The PRIME 'MINISTER. It seems to me that these objections came at a very late hour. The committee proceeded as all committees have proceeded. They kept a record of their proceedings. They first moved in the House that they be authorized to employ stenographers for the purpose of keeping such a record. When the proceedings were completed and the committee had come to a conclusion the suggestion was made by the bon. leader of the opposition to have typed copies made of the proceedings for the members of the committee. Seven copies were made for that purpose. Then, for the information of the House there was a transcription made of the resolutions moved by the hou. leader of the opposition in which they embodied their policy. This was printed and distributed with the Bill. Seven hundred copies of this have been printed, 200 copies have been distributed to the members of the House of Commons and 81 copies to the Senators. It is probable that while members of the House were very much engaged with another Bill they forgot to look in their boxes for their mail and see that they had 1Jhe information. Now, however, I do not want at all to unduly press hon. members on_the other side of the House. If they want to have a little time to consider their piosition very good ; we will adjourn now, but I would suggest to hon. gentlemen opposite that it would be quite fair to pass the resolution in regard to Carleton after the explanation which has been given and we will adjourn immediately afterwards.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
There is one thing I would like to call the right hon. gentleman's attention to before this is passed. I am quite sure the right hon. gentleman wot, d not conclude that it would be possible to bring down a schedule in the first instance and have the opposition assent to that schedule and have it carried through the House. I do not think the right hon. gentleman would say that that was a fair proposition.
I am going to state to him now that the first cast of constituencies brought down by ihon. gentlemen opposite has not in effect been varied one jot or tittle. The constituencies with one member, the constituencies with two members, and the constituencies with three members as embodied in the first cast are to-day embodied in the Bill. That is a very strong statement to make, but I will ask the Minister of Justice if that statement is not absolutely correct. There is just this variation that instead of Haliburton and Muskoka being together, Victoria and Haliburton are placed together.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
1 repeat the statement that the draft that was made up by the hon. gentlemen opposite in the very first instance, on the 11th of May, has not in substance been altered one jot or tittle. It is as follows :
One member-Glengarry, Prescott, Stormont, Russell, Dundas, Carleton (except Ottawa), Grenville, Frontenac, Kingston, Lennox and Addington, Prince Edward, Durham, Victoria, Peel, Ilalton, Dufferin, Wentworth (except Hamilton), Norfolk, Haldimand, Lincoln, Welland, London, Nipissing, Haliburton and Muskoka, Parry Sound, Thunder Bay.
Two members-Ottawa, Lanark, Leeds, Renfrew, Hastings, Northumberland, Peterborough, Ontario, Wellington, Bruce, Perth, Waterloo, Hamilton, Brant, Oxford, Elgin, Lambton, Kent, Essex, Algoma.
Three members-Simcoe, York, Grey, Huron, Middlesex (except London).
That was the draft given on the 11th of May and I want to call the right hon. gentleman's attention to this that although the f orm of sitting in the committee has been gone through -it has not been changed one particle as a result of those sittings. If hon. gentlemen opposite were right it has not been changed. If hon. gentlemen were wrong in a single division, it has not been changed. I wish to make that statement before adjournment ; and without contending as to Carleton I think it right that the hon. gentleman should know that this is not a state of things that is likely to happen In a fair division.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: It is only right that this committee should be seized of the manner in which that schedule was prepared. It was after considerable discussion in the committee as to what rules should govern its actions. The hon. member would lead this committee) to believe that this was prepared without any consideration or before any committee meetings were held. This was not the case; it was prepared after several conversations had taken place among the members of the committee and it was not expected to lay down wlipt rules should govern the action of the committee but was simply Intended as a guide and as some foundation upon which to work, something which had been agreed upon and to which we would confine ourselves. The proposition was made out at the instance of the chairman for the Information of all the members of the committee.	*

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
Does the hon. gentleman
say that this was made up after certain deliberations had taken place and after a proposition had come from this side of the House with regard to the unit, &c. ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
I say it was made out after we had several discussions as to the unit and as to the way that unit was to be applied and it was only intended to facilitate business. The memorandum was prepared at the Instance

of the chairman and was submitted to the committee for our information.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: 1 am calling attention to the fact that this is the proposition and it makes no difference when it was produced. It is headed ' proposed redistribution for Ontario, submitted by Liberal members at informal meeting, May 11, 1903,' and these have not been departed from in any one instance. The contention the hon. gentlemen opposite has set forth in it is contained in the Bill with unvarying regularity.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: That is all right, I think we are following the rule laid down and that is all.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: But this was three months before the matter was made public.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: My hon. friend must know that the committee was in session for three months.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: What I say is that not a single one of the propositions submitted from this side of the House was accepted. That is the proposition of the hon. gentlemen and it has been adhered to to the letter.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: The action of the committee should not be misrepresented. What is important is that we have before us the suggestions of the majority of the committee and the suggestions made in a few cases by the minority and the question now is which of these should prevail. I do not know that, there is anything to be gained by recrimination or by attempts to intimate that somebody was improperly Influenced or acted in an improper manner. I think we all endeavoured to do as we thought best and now the propositions in a concrete form are before the committee of this House who can judge for themselves. I wish to say to my friend from Elgin (Mi-. Ingram) who said that these proceedings should have been brought before the House that in inviting members on both sides of this House to appear and make statements, the committee were seeking full information, but these gentlemen are all here now and they can give all that evidence and can add to what they said in the committee anything that would influence the minds of members to make any change.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
Will the hon. minister look around him and see if any of the gentlemen are here filling these empty benches and able to give him any of this information.
Item allowed to stand.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
Before the committee rises may I ask that the work of the committee would be greatly facilitated if it was possible to have this minute of proceedings indexed. I think it is a pity that the proceedings were not printed, but as this was not done it would greatly facilitate the work if they are indexed. I understand the Minister of Justice proposes to have
them indexed and if we had one or two copies indexed it would be of a great use to the committee in the continuation of this work.
Progress reported.

maintopic: ADJOURNEMENT-BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE.

speechtext: The PRIME MINISTER moved the adjournment of the House.

maintopic: ADJOURNEMENT-BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE.
speechtext: Before this motion passes I think I would like to ask the Prime Minister, in the event of our advancing this work considerably to-morrow, what it is intended to take up after we have disposed of the Bill. There is another point to which I would also like to call the hon. gentleman's attention. We would probably enter into a consideration of the Transcontinental Railway Bill next week. I mentioned this morning that it would be very desirable for us to have before the House the railway resolutions before we again enter upon the consideration of that. measure. I am sure my right hon. friend will understand why that is. The Transcontinental Railway will entail a very considerable railway expenditure and I think it is only fair that the House should have before it a statement of what other expenditure in connection with railways is contemplated for this year. I think this resolution and the last estimates should be before the House as soon as possible.

maintopic: ADJOURNEMENT-BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE.
speechtext: I agree. 1 cannot bind myself to any particular day, but it is the intention of the government, especially if we make some reasonable progress, to have these ready at a very early day.
Motion agreed to, and House adjourned at 10.50 p.m.	.
Ottawa, Friday, September 11, 1903.
